In addition, it gave no consideration of whether partial disclosure of any of the records refused under article 8(a)(iv) of the AIE Regulations was possible in line with article 10(5) of the AIE Regulations. The Council also failed to identify any “adverse effect” that would arise as a result of the disclosure of the specific information at issue or any clear link between disclosure of the specific information withheld and any adverse effect. With regard to the confidentiality element of article 8(a)(iv) of the AIE Regulations, other than referencing section 31 of the FOI Act (and additionally Section 32 of the FOI Act in correspondence to this Office), the Council has not adequately provided any specific basis for the confidentiality.
17. Having considered the decision-making records and all correspondence between this Office and the Council on these cases, I find that the Council did not provide adequate reasons for refusal of the records at issue, and, due to that, I cannot find that the Council’s refusal of the information sought is justified under article 8(a)(iv) of the AIE Regulations.
18. Given that the refusal to release records has not been justified, I must now consider whether the identified records should be released to the appellant at this stage, or whether I should direct the Council to carry out a fresh decision-making process. My key considerations in this regard are as follows:
• The limited records made available to this Office for the purpose of this review date from March – April 2020 (in respect of Request 1) and September 2021 (in respect of Request 2). While I accept that investigations of any nature can take time and that investigations of enforcement matters can often prove complex, I also note, in correspondence to this Office, that the Council outlines that these are the only records held by the Council’s Environment Section in relation to these sites. On this basis, it is not clear whether other relevant sections within the Council were consulted in terms of retrieving information which may be relevant to the appellant’s requests.
• Both records identified by the Council as being relevant to the appellant’s request, contain references to third parties. This Office takes the view that procedural fairness requires due consideration to be given to whether any potentially affected third party should be notified and be given an opportunity to make submissions where their interests would potentially be affected by any proposed disclosure of the environmental information under review. There is no indication that the Council gave any consideration to this point.
• Lastly, I note that the Council’s original decisions, which were affirmed at internal review stage “without modification”, included a reference to “section 31(1)(a) Legal Profession Privilege”. It is this Office’s view, that protection for legal professional privilege most appropriately falls for consideration within the exception in article 9(1)(b) of the AIE Regulations, it being a key tenet of the administration of justice. While the Council referred to legal professional privilege, it did not rely on article 9(1)(b) of the AIE Regulations, nor did it provide sufficient submissions or evidence to enable me to assess the applicability of that provision in these appeals.
Conclusion
19. Article 4(5) of the AIE Directive provides that “A refusal to make available all or part of the information requested shall be notified to the applicant … The notification shall state the reasons for the refusal ...’.Taking into account the AIE legislation and relevant case law, in these appeals, I am not satisfied that the Council has substantively and procedurally complied with the requirements of article 4(5) of the AIE Directive, as implemented by the AIE Regulations in articles 7(4), 11(4) and 10(3), (4) and (5) as laid out above. In Right to Know v An Taoiseach
, the Court cited RPS v Kildare County Council
[2016
IEHC 113 ] in relation to the purpose of a right to reasons. The recognition of a legal right to reasons, as a matter of natural justice, constitutional law, under the ECHR, and in EU law, reflects and serves a range of important policy objectives. In summary, reasons enable a person to know whether there are grounds to challenge the decision; enable the decision to be effectively reviewed when challenged; encourage and support better administrative decision-making; and act as a promoter of transparency and a deterrent to arbitrary administrative action or malpractice.
20. Based on all the above, I consider it necessary for the Council to carry out a fresh decision-making process in respect of the records identified. In addition, I expect the Council to set out, for the appellant, information about the steps taken to search for information relevant to the requests along with information about the Council’s records management practices insofar as they relate to the information in question.
21. In re-considering the requests, should the Council wish to rely on article 8(a)(iv) (or any other exemption provision provided for in article 8/9 of the AIE Regulations), it must fully set out its reasons for reaching its conclusions as well as, where relevant, its considerations of article 10 of the AIE Regulations, including paragraphs (3), (4), (5) and, where applicable, (6). It may also be helpful for the Council to review the published decisions that the Commissioner has issued particularly in relation to article 8(a)(iv) and 9(1)(b) (available at
www.ocei.ie
). The Council should also in particular note its obligation in article 10(4) to interpret the exemptions on a restrictive basis having regard to the public interest served by disclosure.
Decision
22. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations on behalf of the Commissioner for Environmental Information, I hereby annul the decision of the Council in both cases. I direct the Council to carry out a fresh internal review process in respect of the appellant’s requests. In doing so, I expect the Council to engage in a comprehensive manner with the provisions of the AIE Regulations, taking into account my comments in this decision and the rights of third parties. Should the appellant remain unsatisfied with the decision of the Council, he will be free to appeal that decision once again to this Office.
Appeal to the High Court
23. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two (2) months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Gemma Farrell
On behalf of the Commissioner for Environmental Information

title: Mr S. & Kerry County Council
text:
Decision
Mr S. & Kerry County Council
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-165129-N2J5R5
Published on 9 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether the Council has carried out adequate searches pursuant to article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations.
9 July 2026
Background
1. On 24 June 2025 the appellant made an AIE request to Kerry County Council (the Council) which concerned the zoning status of a section of Cliffs in Ballybunion. On 14 July 2025 the Council sought to invoke article 9(2)(a) of the AIE Regulations, contending that the request was manifestly unreasonable and seeking engagement from the appellant to refine its scope.
2. On 14 July 2025, the appellant refined the scope of his request to:
“1. All records relating to the rezoning decision
Including:
• The planning report(s) and internal briefing documents that informed or supported the rezoning decision.
• Minutes or summaries of internal meetings (including senior planning staff or management) where the rezoning was discussed.
• Any communications between Fáilte Ireland and the Council regarding the rezoning.
2. All records demonstrating legal and environmental compliance
Including:
• Any related legal or planning advice.
• Any screening reports or assessments undertaken for Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) or Appropriate Assessment (AA) specifically in relation to this rezoning.
Any correspondence or submissions received from the NPWS or other statutory bodies during the plan-making process, specifically referencing this area or the potential impact on the SAC
Do you have a link to any pre-draft submissions or other preliminary public or stakeholder consultations?”.
3. On 19 August 2025 the Council invoked article 7(2)(b) to extend the deadline by which the decision was due to the respondent, by one month.
4. On 13 October 2025 the Council issued its original decision which stated that it was granting the request, it simultaneously relied upon article 7(5) however to refuse access to some elements of the information sought on the basis that it did not hold it; therefore, it is more accurate to state the request was partially granted.
5. The original decision states:
“The planning department have confirmed the Councils website contains all records as part of the Statutory process. The first link previously supplied would have contained the draft records and Material Alterations.
The planning department has identified no records which deal specifically with the change in zoning. The below link to Kerry County Councils website provides the
• Local Area Plan
• SEA Statement
• Natura Impact report
Listowel Municipal District Plan 2020-2026 | kerrycoco.ie
• Minutes of Listowel Municipal District Meeting September 2020 lap20.pdf
Pre-draft consultation was carried out in 2018 (8th Feb 2018 to 23rd March 2018) and the Council received 11 submissions. The planning department have reviewed the submissions. There was no specific submission in relation to Ballybunion settlement. There was no submission from the NPWS or Failte Ireland.
1 Schedule of records
The planning department has reviewed the file in relation to the Listowel Municipal District Local Area Plan 2020-2026. The following records have been identified:
1 LMD SEA Scoping Report issued in April 2018 prior to the plan being prepared.
2 Listowel Scoping Submissions received
3 Version of Ballybunion Maps
o May 2018
o November 2018
o December 2018
o September 2019
o October 2019
o September 2020
The planning department has confirmed the May 2018 map would be the first version prepared when work started on the Draft Local Area Plan. Subsequent versions would include changes to the draft. The planning department has not identified any record outlining the changes between versions.
2 Findings, particulars and reasons for decision to deny access
The sections of the AIE Regulations which can apply to deny access to documents are known as its exemption provisions.
Section 7 of the Regulations sets out
(5) Where a request is made to a public authority and the information requested is not held by or for the authority concerned, that authority shall inform the applicant as soon as possible that the information is not held by or for it.
The Planning department has not identified specific records in relation to the change of zoning of the area identified on the maps provided”.
6. On 16 October 2025 the appellant requested an internal review decision.
7. On 18 November 2025 the Council issued its internal review decision, affirming the original decision.
8. The appellant appealed to this Office on 30 November 2025.
9. I have been directed by the Commissioner to undertake a review under article 12(5) of the Regulations. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by the appellant and the Council. In addition, I have had regard to:
a. the Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (the Minister’s Guidance);
b. Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
c. the 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention); and
d. The Aarhus Convention—An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (‘the Aarhus Guide’).
Scope of Review
10. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, my role is to review the public authority's internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it.
11. My review in this case is concerned with whether the Council has carried out adequate searches pursuant to article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations.
Analysis and Findings
7(5)
12. Article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations is the relevant provision to consider, where the question arises as to whether the requested environmental information or any further environmental information is held by, or for, the public authority concerned. It provides as follows:
“Where a request is made to a public authority and the information requested is not held by or for the authority concerned, that authority shall inform the applicant as soon as possible that the information is not held by or for it.”
13. What will be considered reasonable will vary from case to case, but as a general guide, I set out below the type of information that my Office would generally expect to be set out in a decision where a public authority is relying on article 7(5) of the Regulations:
i. an outline of exactly which areas/units etc. of the organisation were searched for the information.
ii. an explanation of how searches were carried out (i.e. manually, by computer, by name, by key words).
iii. Keywords should be recorded and provided in the decision as appropriate. details of the individuals consulted in connection with the search.
iv. a description of the searches carried out to cover the possibility of misfiled/misplaced records.
v. details of guidelines, practices, procedures and arrangements in relation to the storage, filing, archiving, retention and destruction of the type of information requested in this case.
14. In this case the appellant is not satisfied that the Council have conducted adequate searches pertaining to all information falling within the scope of the request, with particular emphasis on the Council’s statement that it does not hold any records in relation to any change in the zoning status of the area to which the request concerns. The appellant notes that the Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) report with respect to the area in question, released as part of the AIE request, identifies the “environmental factors to be considered for the Local Area Plan” however that it “does not demonstrate that environmental legislation was applied or that the rezoning decision was informed by the SEA process”.
15. The appellant further describes the Council’s submission that the land rezoning may have resulted from changes in Tailte Éireann background mapping, as “not credible”
, contending that “…a cartographic update cannot justify altering zoning within a Natura 2000 site. Even if the cliffs appeared differently on the updated map, any resulting change to zoning layers would have required internal instructions, discussions, and environmental checks. The assertion that no such records exist is inconsistent with normal planning processes”.
16. In its submission to this Office, the Council contend that it has undertaken satisfactory searches to identify records pertaining to the information sought. With respect to the land in question, it states:
“The Planning Dept. has reviewed its files and does not have any additional records that it can provide. All relevant material relating to the adoption of the Listowel Municipal District Local Area Plan 2020-2026 has been provided. There are no other records in relation to the zoning of individual plots of land or amendments to zonings/settlement boundaries prior to the publication of the Draft LAP which was published on October 31st, 2019. The box file/hard copies in relation to this Local Area Plan are available for inspection in the Planning Dept. Our digital files have also been reviewed and apart from different versions of zoning maps, which have been provided, there are no records/documents in relation to changes made from one version to the next”.
Detailing associated searches, it notes:
“All relevant folders which contain plans have been searched. All documentation containing the records are held on the hard drive under M:\Planning_New\PPolicy\Forward_Planning\Municipal District Plans\4.Listowel There would be no mobile phone messages and emails (the plan was prepared in 2019). We have searched emails for “cliff” and no relevant results for Ballybunion”.
17. With respect to the appellant’s request for records relating to submissions on the draft consultation and legal and environmental compliance, it states:
“Kerry County Council did not receive submissions from Fáílte Ireland in relation to the Listowel MD LAP. A submission from Fáilte Ireland was therefore not received on the Draft LAP or in relation to pre-draft consultation which took place early 2018. We provided copies of the various Environmental Assessments, SEA Scoping report and versions of Ballybunion Maps.
The NPWS did not make a submission on the Draft LAP. SEA Scoping took place in April/May 2018. The NPWS also did not make a submission on the SEA Scoping. Kerry County Council provided copies of the various Environmental Assessments, SEA Scoping report and versions of Ballybunion Maps.
Website links provided to Mr S. contained all records as part of the Statutory process; this would have included the draft records and material alterations. The planning department has identified no records which deal specifically with the change in zoning.
Links were also provided which detailed:
• Local Area Plan
• SEA Statement
• Natura Impact report
• Minutes of Listowel Municipal District Meeting September 2020”.
18. In reviewing the appellant’s submission with respect to his appeal, I note his contentions with respect to the legal context of re-zoning land, to include obligations on public bodies pursuant to the Habitats Directive, SEA Directive, and Planning and Development Act 2000. I also acknowledge information he has provided regarding historical FOI requests to the Council for information relevant to this appeal and his position with respect to the connection between the land in question and other Council records to include the Ballybunion draft Development Plan July 2020 and the Kerry County Tourism Strategy and Action Plan 2026-2022
.
19. It is my view that in this case the appellant’s contentions that further information and records exist, arises in the context of an expectation of information a public authority would be expected to have if it undertook an exercise to re-zone land, according to legal and environmental obligations. These contentions are outlined further by the appellant in the context of his previous FOI requests which yielded other records he suggests are relevant and, adjacent Council documents which concern the townland and area (to include the zoned land in question).
20. In considering the above, I have also reviewed the submission from the Council which is consistent with its reasoning at original and internal review stage that no further records are held with respect to the zoned land in question, either by or for it. It is the Council’s position that no re-zoning has taken place, attributing the variation in maps to “mapping changes”,
further stating in its internal review decision that “Kerry County Council use Tailte Éireann as background maps to which to place zoning maps over. There was a significant change in the style of maps used between the Tailte Éireann background map used in 2020 and the map used in 2013. Tailte Éireann show the cliffs as ‘Sand, sand and shingle” and “embankment”.
21. In reviewing the Council’s search details concerning the information being sought, outlined at paragraph 16 and 17 I am persuaded that adequate searches have been undertaken such to reasonably conclude that further information is not held by or for it. This belief stems from my consideration of the nature of the information itself, the locations searched/search terms used and, the relevance of the Council’s view that no re-zoning has taken place, but rather that the difference may be attributed to historical mapping data. Notwithstanding my view that the search information provided has met the threshold of 7(5) in this case, I find it logical to assume that if the Council are of the view that the land was not re-zoned, then information and records associated with a re-zoning process are not held by or for it.
22. While it is the appellant’s view that this information should exist, it is outside the remit of this Office to adjudicate on how public authorities carry out their functions generally, including with respect to their environmental information management practices. I have no role in assessing how public authorities collect, maintain and disseminate environmental information. My role concerns reviewing appeals of requests for access to environmental information within the scope of the request, which is held by or for the relevant public authority and no more than that.
23. Indeed, if this land has in fact been rezoned then the appellant is correct to assert and expect specific legal and environmental activities and therefore records, to exist, however the question of whether this has taken place, and accordingly whether it ought to have taken place, is outside of the remit of this Office.
24. The information the Council have provided at internal decision stage and within its submission to this Office with respect to searches undertaken, combined with its position that the information does not exist as it was not legally necessary to produce, leads me to reasonably conclude that it has met its obligations under article 7(5).
Decision
25. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I affirm the Council’s decision.
Appeal to the High Court
26. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Gemma Farrell
Senior Investigator
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information

title: Mr. X & Coillte
text:
Decision
Mr. X & Coillte
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-160332-H2V7Y5
Published on 8 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether Coillte was justified in refusing the appellant’s request on the basis that no further environmental information within the scope of that request is held by or for it.
08 July 2026
Background
1. On 17 April 2025 the appellant made a request to Coillte under the AIE Regulations seeking access to the following information:
“Information that demonstrates that the use of fertilisers on sites where exotic coniferous species dominate is equally or more ecologically beneficial than the use of silvicultural systems that do not require fertilizers.”
2. On 16 May 2025, Coillte issued its original decision which refused access to the requested information in reliance of Article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations, wherein the decision maker stated that “the information sought does not exist and therefore is not “held” by or for Coillte”.
3. The appellant sought an internal review of the decision on 19 May 2025.
4. Coillte issued its internal review decision on 18 June 2025, advising that following re-examination of the request that the decision made by the initial decision maker should be affirmed.
5. The appellant submitted an appeal to this Office on 04 July 2025.
6. I have now completed my review of this appeal under article 12(5) of the Regulations. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by the appellant and by Coillte. In addition, I have had regard to:
• the Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (the Minister’s Guidance);
• Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
• the 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention); and
• The Aarhus Convention—An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (‘the Aarhus Guide’).
7. What follows does not comment or make findings on each and every argument advanced, but all relevant points have been considered.
Scope of Review
8. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, my role is to review the public authority’s internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it. Where appropriate in the circumstances of an appeal, I will require the public authority to make available environmental information to the appellant.
9. Pursuant to article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations, this review is concerned with whether Coillte was justified in refusing access to the information requested by the appellant on the basis that no further information within the scope of the request is held by Coillte.
Analysis and Findings
10. Article 7(1) of the AIE Regulations requires public authorities to make available environmental information that is held by or for them on request, subject only to the provisions of the AIE Regulations.
11. Article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations is the relevant provision to consider, where the question arises as to whether the requested environmental information or any further environmental information is held by or for the public authority concerned. It provides as follows;
“Where a request is made to a public authority and the information requested is not held by or for the authority concerned, that authority shall inform the applicant as soon as possible that the information is not held by or for it”.
12. This Office’s approach to dealing with this type of case is to assess whether adequate steps have been taken to identify and locate relevant environmental information, having regard to the particular circumstances. In determining whether the steps taken are adequate in the circumstances, a standard of reasonableness is applied.
13. What will be considered reasonable will vary from case to case. Article 7(5) of the AIE regulations allows public authority to refuse a request if it does not hold the requested information. In order for a public authority to successfully rely on this provision, it must, among other things, provide evidence that it carried out adequate searches for the environmental information requested.
14. In its initial submission to this Office, Coillte detailed the searches undertaken, a summary of which I provide as follows:
• the AIE team consulted with two key subject matter experts (SMEs); the Establishment Process Manager, who is responsible for managing and coordinating Establishment operations across all Business Area Units (BAUs), including the application of fertilisers; and the Silvicultural Specialist, who provides technical support to the Establishment Process Manager and oversees various silvicultural research projects and trials aimed at improving forestry practices within Coillte. These discussions focused on whether such information is typically created or retained, and whether searches could be carried out to locate it.
• Coillte stated that the purpose of these searches consultations was twofold: i. to establish whether the type of information sought typically exists and/or is held by Coillte; and ii. to request that the SMEs undertake appropriate searches for any such information, if held.
• The authority further states that “SMEs were advised to conduct comprehensive searches across all relevant storage systems, including cloud-based platforms, Office 365/email systems, and team-based storage. These searches were carried out both electronically and physically, using a range of parameters such as file name, date, and keywords. The keywords/search terms employed included: ‘Exotic Conifer’, ‘Exotic Conifer Fertiliser’, and ‘Exotic Conifer Treatment’.”
• Based on these searches the authority stated that it was “satisfied that reasonable steps were taken to identify any relevant records, and it has been confirmed that no such information is held by or for Coillte”.
15. In relation to whether information relevant to the appellant’s request could be located elsewhere in the organisation Coillte submits that the “likelihood of such records being misfiled or stored outside the relevant business areas is extremely low”,
and “in the unlikely event that a record had been misfiled, it would still be identified through keyword searches conducted across our cloud-based storage systems”.
16. Within his statement of appeal, the appellant provided arguments as to why he believed that information on this subject should exist within Coillte. A summary of this submission is provided as follows:
• The appellant’s request is based on the conditions of the Irish FSC Interim National Standard which came into force on the 15th of July 2024.
• The appellant notes that as a result of information received from Coillte in a previous AIE request, the authority applied “over 1300 tonnes of fertiliser across its estate after the 15th of July 2024”.
• The appellant has provided further text to this Office where he contends that Coillte is a Forest Stewardship Council certificate holder and as such is bound by the standards of that body. One such standard highlighted by the appellant is as follows, “Criteria 10.6 The Organization* shall minimize or avoid the use of fertilizers*. When fertilizers* are used, The Organization* shall demonstrate that use is equally or more ecologically and economically beneficial than use of silvicultural* systems that do not require fertilizers, and prevent, mitigate, and/or repair damage to environmental values*, including soil”.
• As a result of the above the appellant contends that “my request is for information that Coillte would need to be able to evidence compliance to a third-party auditor. Therefore, records should exist. I appreciate that they may not exist, but this would involve a breach of certification standards. I therefore need to be clear that Coillte have taken all reasonable steps to identify the requested information”.
17. At the request of the investigator assigned to this appeal, Coillte provided additional clarification on a number of points which I summarise as follows:
• With regards to the possibility that information relevant to the appellants request may lie with third party contractors the authority states, “contractors are not involved in the design, management, or monitoring of fertiliser trials. Such trials are typically overseen by forestry researchers or relevant state bodies, and contractors would not be expected to hold or generate information relevant to the ecological assessment of fertiliser use in these contexts.”
• In relation to the search terms used the authority stated that both ‘fertiliser’ and ‘fertilizer’ were considered within the search terms as both spellings appear in the appellant’s request.
• Coillte has also confirmed that the silivicultural expert within the authority had returned no search results for the appellants request and the authority noted that the body had “not carried out any research projects or trials involving the non-use of fertiliser inputs and/or silviculture techniques in the establishment and maintenance of conifer plantations”.
• Coillte confirmed that “overall responsibility for fertiliser planning, use and reporting across the Coillte estate lies with the Establishment Process Manager”.
• With regards to the search terms used by the authority, the list initially provided by the authority was not exhaustive and other search terms used were “Exotic Conifer Fertilizer, Conifer Fertiliser / Conifer Fertilizer, Exotic Coniferous Fertiliser / Exotic Coniferous Fertilizer”.
18. In a separate submission to this Office, with regards to the possibility that information relevant to the appellants request may exist within a third party, the authority has further stated that Coillte “has not carried out any research projects or trials involving the non-use of fertiliser inputs and/or silvicultural techniques. Accordingly, there was no necessity to engage with forestry researchers and/or relevant state bodies in relation to such trials, as these have not been undertaken by Coillte.”
19. In order to provide the appellant with an opportunity to respond to the submissions of the authority a summary of these submissions was provide by the investigator in this appeal to which the appellant provided a lengthy response of which I intend to only provide the headings of as follows:
1. Coillte has still not demonstrated what searches were actually undertaken
2. The search terms remain conceptually too narrow
3. Coillte appears to have mischaracterised the request as being about “trials”
4. The focus on only two SMEs has not been justified
5. The response concerning contractors, researchers and state bodies is inadequate
6. The “misfiled records” reasoning is speculative and insufficient
7. There is a clear plausibility basis for expecting records to exist
8. The preliminary position should not be maintained
20. I note that the appellant has raised a number of queries in his appeal on the adequacies of searches carried out by the authority in question in response to his request. Having considered the search details provided, I am persuaded they satisfy what is required in the circumstances of this case. To be clear, article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations does not require a forensic trawling exercise to be conducted by public authorities, rather a test of reasonableness and an adequate search exercise should be performed. This Office does not generally expect public authorities to carry out extensive or indefinite general searches for records simply because an applicant asserts that more records should or might exist, or rejects a public authorises explanation of why a record does not exist.
21. The appellant has expressed concern that the search terms used by Coillte were too narrow. However, Coillte has explained that the keyword searches were not the only search method used. The searches were supplemented by consultation with the relevant subject-matter experts, including the officer with overall responsibility for fertiliser planning, use and reporting. Coillte also confirmed that both “fertiliser” and “fertilizer” were considered, and that broader terms such as “Conifer Fertiliser/Fertilizer” and “Exotic Coniferous Fertiliser/Fertilizer” were used. While it may be possible to identify additional search terms, article 7(5) does not require exhaustive or speculative searching. The question is whether the steps taken were reasonable in the circumstances.
22. Likewise, the appellant has, in his appeal, referred to the participation of the authority in a certification process which in his opinion places an onus on the authority to meet certain criteria of that scheme which may be of relevance to the subject matter of this appeal. The appellant’s position is that, by virtue of its participation in the FSC certification process, Coillte may be expected to demonstrate compliance with Criterion 10.6. However, my role in this appeal is not to determine whether Coillte has complied with FSC certification requirements, or whether records ought to have been created for that purpose. My role is confined to determining whether Coillte has taken reasonable and adequate steps to identify environmental information held by or for it within the scope of the appellant’s AIE request.
23. Having considered the submissions of both parties, I am satisfied that Coillte has taken reasonable and adequate steps to identify and locate information within the scope of the appellant’s request.
Decision
24. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I hereby affirm Coillte’s decision.
Appeal to the High Court
25. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Ger Deering
Commissioner for Environmental Information

title: Ms. X & Coillte
text:
Decision
Ms. X & Coillte
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-149018-B6L2P8
Published on 3 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether Coillte was justified in refusing the request as invalid under the AIE Regulations.
03 July 2026
Background
1. This appeal refers to a request for information made by the appellant to Coillte for information related to its Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). As outlined below, the appellant had previously submitted a similar request for information to Coillte on this same subject.
2. On 30 January 2024, the appellant submitted the following request to Coillte:
“This formal AIE request has regard to AIE/2024/0020. and the decision dated 29 January 2024. In the decision for AIE/2024/0020. I was invited to narrow the range of information requested. The decision maker for AIE/2024/0020 asked that the request (AIE/2024/0020) be refined to SOP(s) that relate to a particular area of Coillte's business. However, no information was provided by the decision maker of AIE/2024/0020 on all the areas of business to which Coillte SOP documents apply. Furthermore, there is no named individual noted on the decision dated 29 January 2024. On 19 January 2024, I asked for the contact details of the party assigned to deal with AIE/2024/0020. I have not received any reply to my email of 19 January 2024.
Noting the above omission by the unnamed decision maker for AIE/2024/0020 and to formalise matters under the AIE Regulations further to my informal email of earlier today (submitted at 08.46), please provide, by email, information on all areas of Coillte's business to which Coillte's SOP documents apply”.
3. It should be noted in her request the appellant invoked article 7(10) of the AIE Regulations which requires a public authority to “have regard to any timescale specified by the applicant”. As such, the appellant requested that the authority provide the information requested no later than 20 February 2024.
4. On 01 March 2024 the appellant, having not received a reply to her original request for information, requested an internal review of this deemed refusal from the authority.
5. The appellant, heaving received no reply form the authority to her request for an internal review, made an appeal to this Office on the 16 April 2024.
6. This Office wrote to Coillte to request that it provide the appellant with a statement of reasons for its position in relation to the deemed refusal of the appellant`s request at both the original and internal review stage. On 01 May 2024, Coillte provided the appellant with a statement of reasons for its effective position in not processing the aforementioned request for internal review under the provision of the AIE Regulations.
7. Coillte in its statement of reasons set out as follows: “The OCEI have furnished us with your appeal letter of 02 April 2024 and an email thread with two emails from you to info@coillte.ie. In particular the email thread contains your email to Coillte of 30 January 2024 which we understand now to be the communication which you deem to have been a valid AIE Request pursuant to European Communities (Access to Information on the Environment) Regulations 2007 to 2018 (S.I. No. 133 of 2007, S.I. No. 662 of 2011, S.I. 615 of 2014 and S.I. No. 309 of 2018) (the “AIE Regulations”). Your email of 30 January 2024 was sent on the day after Coillte issued a Request to Refine letter, the 29 April 2024, to you in relation to a request which we have processed under reference AIE20240020. The information requested under AIE20240020 was as follows:
“Please provide, by email, the name and SOP number of all Standard Operating Procedures currently available for use by Coillte. I attach as an example, SOP-049. What I am requesting under this AIE request is information on all such SOP documents which information will comprise the following, as an example: SOP-049 - Procedure for Managing Natural Regeneration in Environmental Setbacks. For the efficiency of the process a public authority should not be required to respond to a subsequent request for information that is identical or substantially similar to a previous request and/or a request that is currently being reviewed by the OCEI, unless a reasonable amount of time has passed since the previous request or the information has changed between the date of the first AIE request and subsequent AIE request.”
The contents of the email of 30 January 2024 cannot reasonably be accepted as an AIE Request raised in the course of dealing with AIE20240020 and effectively repeating that Request by stating “…..please provide, by email, information on all areas of Coillte's business to which Coillte's SOP documents apply” after criticising the manner in which Coillte had issued the Request to Refine and seemingly incorrectly identifying the Request to Refine as Decision letter referring to same as “the decision dated 29 January 2024.
You state the following in your appeal letter: - “The decision maker for AIE/2024/0020 asked that the request (AIE/2024/0020) be refined to SOP(s) that relate to a particular area of Coillte's business. However, no information was provided by the decision maker of AIE/2024/0020 on all the areas of business to which Coillte SOP documents apply. Furthermore, there is no named individual noted on the decision dated 29 January 2024. On 19 January 2024, I asked for the contact details of the party assigned to deal with AIE/2024/0020. I have not received any reply to my email of 19 January 2024.” It should be noted that there is no requirement under the AIE Regulations for a Request to Refine to be issued by a named staff member of a public authority. A timeline in relation to AIE20240020 will assist in clarifying Coillte’s effective position in not processing your request for internal review. The following timeline is relevant: - 17.01.24 AIE Submitted; 19.01.24 Coillte acknowledge AIE ref: 20240020; 29.01.24 Coillte issued Refinement Request 30.01 Email from Ms Walshe as attached to OCEI email; 15.02.24 Further information received from Ms Walshe which has been accepted as a refinement of request by Coillte; 27.02.24 Ann Walshe seeking reply re: email that issued to Coillte on the 15.02.24; 28.02.24 Ann Walshe informed by Coillte that a decision will issue by 15.03.24; 15.03.24 Decision issued on AIE20240020; 26.03.24 Internal review requested. 26.04.24 Internal review decision letter issued on AIE20240020. The contents of your email of 30 January 2024, in terms of the query you raise therein on the subject matter of Coillte SOPs, is deemed by Coillte to be substantially similar to the request processed under AIE20240020.
For the efficiency of the process, a public authority should not be required to respond to a subsequent request for information that is identical or substantially similar to a previous request and/or a request that is currently being reviewed by the OCEI, unless a reasonable amount of time has passed since the previous request or the information has changed between the date of the first AIE request and subsequent AIE request. In this instance the correct and fair procedure is for you to consider the Decision and Internal Review Decision properly issued under AIE20240020 and if unsatisfied thereafter you should submit an appeal to the OCEI. Otherwise, a situation may arise where there are two appeals before the OCEI on the same subject matter within a very short period of time. For the efficiency and integrity of all processes, and the proper allocation of resources, this would be unsatisfactory and ultimately diminish the quality of decision making applied to the subject matter. Coillte, therefore, does not accept the contents of the email of 30 January 2024 as a valid AIE Request and accordingly has not issued a Decision nor an Internal Review Decision.
We reiterate our suggestion that you consider the contents of the Internal Review Decision in AIE20230020 which issued to you last Friday, 26 April 2024, and if you remain unsatisfied, you may submit an appeal to the OCEI under Article 12 of the AIE Regulations. The contents of this letter comprise Coillte’s effective position on the procedural query referred by the OCEI and it is (sic) not intended to be an Internal Review Decision for the purposes of Article 11 of the AIE Regulations.”
8. I have now completed my review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by the appellant and Coillte. In addition, I have had regard to:
(a) Directive 2003/4/EC, upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
(b) United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention);
(c) The Aarhus Convention: An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014); and
(d) the Guidance provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on implementation of the Regulations.
9. What follows does not comment or make findings on each and every argument advanced, but I have considered all materials submitted in the course of the investigation.
Scope of Review
10. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, my role is to review the public authority’s internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it. Where appropriate, I may require a public authority to make available environmental information to the appellant.
11. For clarification the appeal currently before this Office relates to “information on all areas of Coillte's business to which Coillte SOP documents apply.” As outlined above the appellant had previously submitted a separate request for information to Coillte seeking information on “the name and SOP number of all SOPs currently available for use by Coillte.”
12. In this appeal, Coillte refused the appellant`s request for information on the basis that it was not a valid request. The scope of this appeal is confined to whether Coillte were justified in deeming this not to be a valid request under the AIE Regulations.
Analysis and Findings
13. The right of access to information under the AIE Directive is set out in Article 3(1), which states that:
“Member States shall ensure that public authorities are required, in accordance with the provisions of this Directive, to make available environmental information held by or for them to any applicant at his request and without his having to state an interest.” An applicant is defined in Article 2(5) as “any natural or legal person requesting environmental information”.
14. Article 3(5) of the AIE Directive provides:
“For the purposes of this Article, Member States shall ensure that:
(a) officials are required to support the public in seeking access to information;
(b) lists of public authorities are publicly accessible; and
(c) the practical arrangements are defined for ensuring that the right of access to environmental information can be effectively exercised, such as:
— the designation of information officers;
— the establishment and maintenance of facilities for the examination of the information required,
— registers or lists of the environmental information held by public authorities or information points, with clear indications of where such information can be found.”
15. Article 6 of the AIE Regulations, which seeks to transpose Article 3 of the AIE Directive, defines a request for the purpose of the AIE Regulations. Article 6(1) provides that “a request for environmental information shall
:
a. be made in writing or electronic form
,
b. state that the request is made under these Regulations
,
c. state the name, address and any other relevant contact details of the applicant
,
d state, in terms that are as specific as possible, the environmental information that is the subject of the request, and
e. if the applicant desires access to environmental information in a particular form or manner, specify the form or manner of access desired
”
16. Based on the evidence before me, I consider that the appellant’s request complied with the above requirements and therefore was a valid request under the Regulations. Coillte do not appear to be disputing the absence or otherwise of any element of article 6(1) in relation to the appellant’s request. The AIE Regulations do not otherwise provide for a public authority to deem a request invalid where perceived similarities are identified between requests for information albeit from the same appellant.
17. A public authority is required to consider any request that satisfies the above requirements, and provide access to the information sought, or refuse the request where grounds exist under the AIE Regulations to do so.
18. Accordingly, I am not persuaded that Coillte was correct in its interpretation of the AIE Regulations when it found the appellant’s request to be invalid. It is my opinion that the authority should have considered the request in full under the AIE Regulations and provided the appellant with a reasoned response at the original decision stage and if necessary, thereafter at the internal review decision stage.
19. In my consideration of this appeal, it is clear from the evidence provided to this Office by both parties that the appellant has provided sufficient detail to the authority in support of her application under the AIE Regulations for that application to be considered valid under the aforementioned AIE Regulations.
20. As the above was the main ground upon which the appellant’s request was refused, I find that the refusal of the appellant’s request was not justified by the reasons given by Coillte.
21. It may be helpful to note that while I have found that Coillte were not justified in deeming this request to be invalid, it is open to Coillte to apply other provisions if it deems it appropriate to do so. To this end I note the Commissioner’s comments in the 2025 annual review: “A public authority may refuse to make environmental information available where the request is manifestly unreasonable having regard to the volume or range of information sought. In cases where a requester sends multiple communications to a public authority over a short time, there are certain circumstances where some of these separate communications may reasonably be considered to constitute a single request, or a smaller number of requests. The Minister’s Guidance states that article 9(2) of the AIE Regulations clarifies that a public authority may refuse to make information available if the request is considered unreasonable. Both public authorities and requesters should seek to liaise constructively with a view to fully processing the request as efficiently as possible.”
Decision
22. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I find that the authority was not justified in refusing the request as invalid under article 6(1) of the AIE Regulations. I therefore annul Coillte’s decision not to process the AIE request and direct it to process the appellant’s request in accordance with the AIE Regulations and issue a fresh decision.
Appeal to the High Court
23. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Gemma Farrell
On behalf of the Commissioner for Environmental Information

title: Ms. X & Roscommon County Council
text:
Decision
Ms. X & Roscommon County Council
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-300060-A0A2W1
Published on 1 July 2026
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether the Council was justified in refusing access to the requested information under Article 9(2)(c) of the AIE Regulations
01 July 2026
Background
1. On 21 November 2025, the appellant submitted a request to the Council seeking access to;
“Roscommon Co. Co. Lough Funshinagh Statement Monday 3 Nov 2025
The dual project objectives are managing the flood risk and minimising the impact on the environment in this area.
As part of the process, the consultants have identified additional constraints on the emerging preferred route that, in line with best practice, warrants reassessment of all options."
“I wish to have a copy of the additional constraints on the emerging preferred route which are referred to in the councils statement of 03.11.2025”.
2. On 10 December 2025, the Council issued its decision and refused the request under article 9(2)(c) of the AIE regulations.
3. On 18 December 2025, the appellant sought an internal review of the Council’s decision.
4. On 21 January 2026, the Council issued its internal review decision and in doing so affirmed the original decision.
5. On 6 February 2026, the appellant appealed to my Office.
6. I am directed by the Commissioner to carry out a review under article 12(5) of the Regulations. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by the appellant and the Council. I have also examined the contents of the record at issue. In addition, I have had regard to:
a. the Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (the Minister’s Guidance);
b. Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
c. the 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention); and
d. The Aarhus Convention—An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (‘the Aarhus Guide’).
7. What follows does not comment or make findings on each and every argument advanced but all relevant points have been considered.
Scope of Review
8. In accordance with article 12 (5) of the AIE Regulations, the role of this Office is to review the public authority’s internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it. The scope of this review is to determine whether the Council was justified in refusing access to the requested record under article 9(2)(c) of the AIE Regulations.
Analysis and Findings
Article 9(2)(c)
9. Article 9(2)(c) of the AIE Regulations provides that a public authority may refuse to make environmental information available where the request concerns material in the course of completion, or unfinished documents or data. This provision transposes Article 4(1)(d) of the AIE Directive, which in turn is based on part of Article 4(3)(c) of the Aarhus Convention. I consider that the purpose of this exemption is to give public authorities time and private space to draft and amend documents that they are preparing before they are finalised. The European Commission acknowledged this interest in its First Proposal for the AIE Directive, as did the Court of Justice of the European Union in Case C 619/19 Land Baden-Württemberg v. D.R. at paragraph 44.
10. This exemption is not harm-based. It is not necessary for the public authority to show that there is any adverse effect in respect of the release of the information at issue to engage the exemption, just that the information concerns material in the course of completion, or unfinished documents or data. When relying on Article 9 (2)(c) public authorities must also consider the public interest in release of the records in question.
11. Article 9(2)(c) of the AIE Regulations must be read alongside article 10 of the AIE Regulations. Article 10(3) of the AIE Regulations requires a public authority to consider each request on an individual basis and weigh the public interest served by disclosure against the interest served by refusal. Article 10(4) of the AIE Regulations provides that the grounds for refusal of a request shall be interpreted on a restrictive basis having regard to the public interest served by disclosure. Article 10(5) of the AIE Regulations provides that nothing in articles 8 or 9 shall authorise a public authority not to make available environmental information which, although held with information to which article 8 or 9 relates, may be separated from such information. Article 10(6) of the AIE Regulations states that where a request is refused pursuant to article 9(2)(c) because it concerns material in the course of completion, the public authority shall inform the applicant of the name of the authority preparing the material and the estimated time needed for completion.
12. Although the concepts of ‘material in the course of completion’ and ‘unfinished documents or data’ are not defined [by the AIE Directive], it is apparent from the explanations relating to Article 4 of the Proposal for a Directive of the European Parliament and of the Council on public access to environmental information presented by the Commission on 29 June 2000 (COM(2000) 402 final) (OJ 2000 C 337 E, p. 156) that the purpose of that exception is to meet the need of the public authorities to have a protected space in which to pursue internal considerations and debates (see, to that effect, judgment of 20 January 2021, Land Baden-Württemberg (Internal communications), C-619/19, EU:C:2021:35, paragraph 44). The Court has also held, that provided for in point (d) of the first subparagraph of Article 4(1) of the directive relates to the preparation or drafting of documents and is therefore of a temporary nature (see, to that effect, judgment of 20 January 2021, Land Baden-Württemberg (Internal communications), C-619/19, EU:C:2021:35, paragraph 56).
13. Accordingly, the first question to be addressed is whether or not article 9(2)(c) of the AIE Regulations is engaged on the basis that the information at issue “concerns material in the course of completion, or unfinished documents or data” (i.e. which limb(s) of the exemption is being relied upon).
14. It is this Office’s view that “material in the course of completion” relates to the process of preparing information/documents. The Aarhus Guide states that “the expression ‘in the course of completion’ relates to the process of preparation of the information or the document and not to any decision-making process for the purpose of which the given information or document has been prepared.” However, this Office considers that the factual circumstance of each case is relevant to assess and considers that this exemption may apply in two ways, firstly to information that is itself in the course of completion or unfinished, but secondly to information that while not itself material in the course of completion or unfinished, sufficiently concerns the material in the course of completion or unfinished information.
15. I consider that “material in the course of completion” refers to the process of preparing “material” that is itself being actively worked on (just because something is labelled “draft” does not necessarily mean it is “in the course of completion”). However, while information no longer being actively worked on may not itself be “material in the course of completion” it may concern material in the course of completion. In assessing whether the information at issue concerns “material in the course of completion”, I am of the view that it is necessary to identify material that is actively being worked upon, be able to explain why and how the information at issue concerns that material, and consider whether the information at issue is a separate and independent piece of work to that material – if the information at issue is a separate and independent piece of work, the exception will not be applicable. I also consider that the material that is actively being worked upon must have a physical existence (it cannot be something that does not have a physical existence (e.g. a project, exercise or process, although it can be part of same). For example, an overarching project, even if it is not complete, cannot be considered to be “material in the course of completion”, however individual documents that form part of the project might be if they have not yet been completed.
16. As set out in the Aarhus Convention, in the course of completion relates to preparing information or documents and not to a decision-making process the information or documents has been prepared for. In Roheline Kogukond MTÜ, the fact that information was to be used to inform further reports did not render it “material in the course of completion”. The completed requests and reports completed on foot of the requests are separate and independent pieces of work.
17. Having examined the record at issue, I accept that it is labelled as a draft document. However, the fact that a document is labelled ‘draft’ does not establish that it constitutes material in the course of completion. In order to rely on article 9(2)(c), a public authority must identify the material said to be in the course of completion and provide a basis upon which it can be concluded that the material is actively being worked on and remains unfinished. The Council have not explained what aspects of the report remain incomplete, whether further revisions will be made or the extent to which the findings contained within the report may change.
18. The Council submits the “The sole record falling within the scope of the AIE request is a draft consultant report prepared as part of the ongoing optioneering and assessment process for the Lough Funshinagh Climate Adaptation Project. The report is clearly marked ‘Draft 2’ and expressly states that it is not intended for, and should not be relied upon by, any third party.”
“The public interest in protecting the integrity of an ongoing scientific and technical assessment process and ensuring that incomplete or preliminary information is not released in a manner that could mislead or confuse the public. The development of this report will ultimately conclude in the preparation of an application for consent to An Coimisiún Pleanála”.
“The information may be considered for release once the relevant assessment work has been completed and finalised but this is certainly not the case at present.
19. I note the appellants submission “Public access to relevant information is most beneficial while studies are ongoing, as this is when informed members of the public can actively participate in shaping the decision-making process”.
I accept there is a significant public interest in ensuring access to environmental information at a stage where it can facilitate meaningful participation in environmental decision making. While article 9(2)(c) recognises public authorities may require temporary protection for unfinished material, that exception mut be interpreted restrictively in accordance with article 10(4) of the AIE regulations.
20. I also note the appellant did not seek access to all material relating to the project but specifically requested access to “the additional constraints on the emerging preferred route”
referred to in the Council’s statement of the 3 November 2025. The Council has not addressed whether these constraints constitute information capable of being separated from any unfinished material, as required by article 10(5) of the AIE regulations.
21. While the Council have argued the report is labelled as a draft and the report states “it is not intended for, and should not be relied upon by, any third party”.
I would note a number of reports have been published by the Council which have been prepared by the same environmental consultants, Arup, and each have contained the same caveat. I note the Council’s submission states “the release of draft or incomplete material presents a real risk of misinterpretation and undermining ongoing legal and decision-making processes”.
However, I do not consider this to be a relevant factor when applying article 9(2)(c) of the AIE Regulations to requested information. I consider that a requestor is capable of understanding that a draft document may be subject to change and that it is open to a public authority to provide context with information when it is being released.
22. The Council submits;
“At the time of the decision on the AIE request, the report formed part of a live and ongoing technical and environmental assessment process, including:
• Further water quality monitoring;
• Refinement of modelling assumptions;
• Consideration of alternative options; and
• Ongoing consultation with statutory environmental bodies.”
23. In my view these ongoing assessments relate to the project as a whole and not to the individual report in question.
24. While the flood relief solution for Lough Funshinagh is undoubtedly an ongoing project and the report in question may inform future project considerations there is nothing advanced by the Council to indicate that the report itself is unfinished. In my view the record withheld is a separate and independent piece of work to the flood relief solution for Lough Funshinagh. The fact a document may subsequently be used to inform future reports or the decision making process around that project does not render that document material in the course of completion.
25. I am not satisfied the Council have demonstrated the record at issue constitutes material in the course of completion within the meaning of article 9(2)(c) of the AIE regulations. While the report is a labelled as a draft the Council has not established that the report itself remains actively in the course of completion or if the requested information could be separated from the report. I find, therefore, that article 9(2)(c) of the AIE Regulations is not engaged. In the circumstances, I am not required to go on and consider article 10 of the AIE Regulations.
26. I would note the central goal of the AIE regime is to enable effective public participation in environmental decision making. In this case the Council has sought public consultation on the project while refusing access to a record which could facilitate that consultation. While this does not determine the application of article 9(2)(c) it does underpin the need for the exception to be interpreted restrictively.
27. For the above reasons, I find the Council was not justified in relying on article 9(2)(c) in this case. However, in the circumstances it is not appropriate for me to direct release of the information at this stage. Having reviewed the record (an 81 page document) which has been refused in full, article 9(2)(c) appears to have been applied in a blanket manner without due consideration of article 10(5). I note the record at issue contains information, which on the face of it, could potentially engage other exemptions including provisions concerned with the protection of the environment to which that information relates, which would have an adverse effect on the environment if it was released. If the Council intends to apply this, or any other exemption provided for in the AIE Regulations to refuse the requested information, it is required to set out its reasoning, having due regard to the public interest balancing test as required by article 10(3) and 10(4), and the separability requirement in article 10(5).
Decision
28. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I annul the Council’s decision and direct the Council to undertake a fresh decision making process in accordance with the provisions of the AIE Regulations.
Appeal to the High Court
29. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Gemma Farrell
On behalf of the Commissioner for Environmental Information

title: Mr Ken Foxe & Department of Defence
text:
Decision
Mr Ken Foxe & Department of Defence
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-161681-D8T6P9
Published on 26 June 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether the Department was justified in refusing access to information relating to air taxi services hired by the Department on behalf of the President in 2023, 2024, and 2025 under the AIE Regulations.
25 June 2026
Background
1. On 3 July 2025, the appellant submitted a request to the Department, seeking access to: “a record/spreadsheet/database of all air taxi services hired by the department on behalf of the President in 2023, 2024, 2025 to include the date, minute time on board, the route, the department, the number of passengers, and the cost of the service.”
2. The appellant also included the following comments: “I note in the recent FOI decision that reference was made to the Supreme Court judgment concerning the President. However, the Supreme Court judgment has absolutely no bearing on public authorities apart from the President's Office and the Council of State. It does not have any crossover whatsoever to the Department of Defence, against which legal action can be taken. This has already been decided upon by the CEI in previous decisions concerning the use of the Gulfstream jet, which were accepted by the Department of Defence and not appealed to the High Court.”
3. On 5 August 2025, the Department issued its decision, refusing the appellant’s request. It included the following summary of its decision, “[t]his decision is primarily based on the definitive ruling of the Supreme Court ([2022] IESC 19) which affirmed the constitutional immunity of the President for information, including those made under AIE Regulations, irrespective of which public body might hold the information.”
4. The Department also commented “In accordance with Article 10(3) and 10(4) I have weighed the public interest served by disclosure against the interest served by refusal of your request. I have determined that the interest served by refusal outweighs the public interest in disclosure.”
5. However, the Department also went on to acknowledge the Commissioner’s previous decision (CEI/16/0041) which concerned a request for environmental information related to flights undertaken by the Ministerial Air Transport Service, specifically those involving the President. The Department stated that in that case the Commissioner found that the Department of Defence was obliged to disclose environmental information relating to the President's flights and the reasoning underpinning that decision was that Article 3(2) of the AIE Regulations (which excludes certain bodies from the definition of "public authority") did not apply to the Department of Defence.
6. The Department stated “This meant that even if the information related to the President, the Department, as a public authority, still had an obligation to process the AIE request. The OCEI held that information on the dates of travel, departure point and destination, flying time, and the number of passengers is environmental information.”
The Department submitted, however, that decision predates and was fundamentally impacted by the judgment of the Supreme Court of April 29, 2022 which “definitely clarified the scope of the President’s constitutional immunity under Article 13.8.1 of the Constitution of Ireland.”
7. The Department’s view is that the Supreme Court judgment “effectively overruled the interpretation presented in CEI/16/0041 concerning the President’s immunity in the context of AIE Requests”,
establishing that the President’s constitutional immunity extends to AIE requests, the President’s Office is not a “public authority” under AIE, and any attempt to obtain information that would effectively make the President “answerable to the courts”, even if held by another public authority, is precluded by the Constitution. The Department concluded: “In light of the binding precedent set by the Supreme Court, I have concluded that the disclosure of information related to the President’s official acts and functions, as sought in your request, would be contrary to the public interest and would undermine the constitutional immunity afforded to the President.”
8. Also on 5 August 2025, the appellant sought an internal review of that decision. The appellant submitted “The Supreme Court judgment has no application outside of the President, the Secretary General to the President, and the Council of State. It does none of the things described in your decision letter which is based on a misunderstanding of the extent of the judgment. The decision is not supported by any extracts from the judgment, nor could it be, because the judgment does not touch on the issue of records held by other public bodies as in this case.”
9. On 19 August 2025, the Department issued its internal review decision, affirming its original decision. It reiterated that it was refusing access to the information sought on the grounds of the Supreme Court ruling. It stated that it was satisfied that “the constitutional immunity of the President prevents this Department from releasing, under the AIE Regulations, information concerning air travel arranged, on request, on behalf of the President.”
10. On 20 August 2025, the appellant submitted an appeal to this Office of the Department’s decision. He cited the Commissioner’s previous decision in CEI/16/0041 and noted his assertion that the Department “is misinterpreting the recent Supreme Court judgment, which has no application outside of the Office of the President and the Council of State.”
11. I have carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations. In so doing, I have had regard to the correspondence between the Department and the appellant as outlined above and to correspondence between my Office and both the Department and the appellant on the matter. I have also considered a sample of the information sought. In addition, I have had regard to:
• the Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (the Minister’s Guidance);
• Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
• the 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention); and
• The Aarhus Convention—An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (the Aarhus Guide)
• Right to Know CLG v Commissioner for Environmental Information and others [2022] IESC 19 ] (“the President case”)
12. What follows does not comment or make findings on each and every argument advanced but all relevant points have been considered.
Scope of Review
13. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, my role is to review the public authority’s internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it. Where appropriate in the circumstances of an appeal, I will require the public authority to make available environmental information to the appellant.
14. A review by this Office is considered to be de novo, which means that it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of this decision.
15. It is clear from the comments of the Court of Appeal in Redmond & Another v Commissioner for Environmental Information & Another
[2020
IECA 83 ] , at paragraph 51, that the nature of a review by this Office is inquisitorial, rather than adversarial in nature. The extent of the inquiry is determined by this Office and not by the parties to the appeal.
16. In its original and internal review decisions, the Department refused access to the information sought on the grounds of the Supreme Court ruling the President
case and the “constitutional immunity of the President”
. It was not entirely clear from the Department’s original decision or its internal review decision which provisions of the AIE Regulations were being relied upon to refuse the information. This is unsatisfactory.
17. The Department has since clarified its position in its submissions to this Office, which stated that it was relying on article 3(2) of the AIE Regulations to refuse access on the basis that the request is seeking information indirectly from the President, who is not a public authority (I understand the Department’s view to be that this means that the Department is not a public authority in respect of the request), in addition to relying on exemptions under articles 8(a)(ii) and 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations.
18. The Investigator informed the appellant that the Commissioner conducts a fresh review of all aspects of an appeal and is not bound to follow his previous decisions. She summarised and invited the appellant to respond to the Department’s submissions, in particular those that she considered were relevant to the assessment of 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations.
19. In the circumstances, I am satisfied the scope of this review concerns whether the Department was justified in refusing access to information relating to air taxi services hired by the Department on behalf of the President in 2023, 2024, and 2025 under the AIE Regulations, on the basis that it is not a public authority in respect of the request and/or on the basis of article 8(a)(ii) or 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations.
Preliminary Matters
20. The appellant has referred to the prior decision of this Office in CEI/16/0041
Right to Know CLG and Department of Defence
, in which my predecessor decided that the Department was a public authority in respect of the same type of information. He found that the information requested was held by the Department within the meaning of the AIE Regulations and that refusal of access to the information in that case was not justified under articles 8(a)(i), 8(a)(ii) or 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations. That case considered a request to the Department for "a spreadsheet of all travel undertaken by the Ministerial Air Transport Service - to include flights by any aircraft (government jet, Learjet, Beechcraft, Air Corps helicopters etc) - relating (only) to travel by the Presidents Mary McAleese and Michael D Higgins in the period 11 November 1997 to the [date of the request].”
The appellant submits that the matter was fully dealt with in that case and that this appeal should be determined on the same basis. In this regard the appellant has requested that “[g]iven this matter has already been decided by the CEI, I would request that it is dealt with quickly”.
21. I accept that I have a general obligation to act consistently by treating like cases alike, unless there is good reason for not doing so. As will be clear from my decision below, while I continue to be satisfied that the Department is a public authority in relation to the request, I now accept that the Department’s refusal is justified under article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations.
