title: Mr. F. & Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
text:
Decision
Mr. F. & Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-160893-X9S0X9
Published on 16 June 2026
16 June 2026
Background
1. In June 2025, on foot of information received from the Department contained in a decision letter regarding a separate AIE request, the appellant wrote to the Department making the following request “...I am now seeking, under the AIE Regulations, a copy of the draft Sectoral Plan that was submitted to the Department of Housing as stated in the decision. This information must be complete because it was submitted to another public authority. It cannot be refused under Article 9(2)(c).”
2. The record in question is the draft “Forestry Sectoral Action Work Plan”
which was sent from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of Housing in May 2025.
3. The Department replied on 03 July 2025, refusing the information sought under Article 9(2)(c) of the AIE Regulations.
4. The appellant sought an internal review on the same date, as follows:
“I wish to request an internal review of this decision.
I have received a number of 9(2)(c) decisions from you recently and it is clear that there are members of the Department who do not understand the provision. Either that or there is deliberate intent to frustrate and delay my access to environmental information. I respectfully suggest that you review the decisions of the Commissioner on Article 9(2)(c) before issuing your internal review decision.
You are the decision makers, not the Grade 1 Forestry Inspector. It is for you to source the information from him and apply the Regulations as appropriate. You should not be allowing him to make the decision. I will be speaking to the OCEI about this matter.”
5. On 16 July 2025, the Department issued the following internal review decision:
“I have decided on your Internal Review request on 16th July 2025. My decision is to affirm the original decision for the following reasons:
Having reviewed the draft Sectoral Plan document, I can confirm that this document is still incomplete. The document is heavily annotated and there are a one hundred and nine (109) reviewer comments from multiple contributors, from both the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Housing, discussing and debating key paragraphs, as well as tables without any figures or labels. It is evident that this document is incomplete and actively being worked on and there are grounds for refusal of its release under 9(2)(c), as supported by the OCEI decision in the case Mr X and DAA PLC (OCE-108539-Y0R2X8) which states:
“…the explanation of that term in the Aarhus Guide, which notes that “the words ‘in the course of completion suggest that the term refers to individual documents that are actively being worked on by the public authority. Once those documents are no longer in the course of completion they may be released, even if they are still unfinished and even if the decision to which they pertain has not yet been resolved.”
Where information has been refused or partially refused, the following article(s) of SI 133/2007 apply: 9(2)(c) A public authority may refuse to make environmental information available where the request concerns material in the course of completion, or unfinished documents or data.
Searches Conducted in relation to the original AIE request.
Following the assignment of this Internal Review to me, the following searches were undertaken: A searching email was sent to a Grade 1 Forestry Inspector who is a subject matter expert requesting a copy of the finalised draft of the Sectoral Plan which had been submitted to the Department of Housing. The inspector responded to say that the document had yet to be finalised and was still in the course of completion but would be publicly available in Q3 2025.
Searches Conducted in relation to this Internal Review.
A searching email was sent to the Grade 1 Inspector requesting a copy of the Draft Sectoral Plan as it stands in order to ascertain that it was, as a document, not complete in and of itself but an active working document. The inspector provided the rough draft copy of the plan and I reviewed the document and determined that in its current form, it’s release would be premature and potentially misleading by inclusion or exclusion of details that are subject to frequent amendment at this time.”
6. The appellant submitted an appeal to this Office on 25 July 2025. In his submission he stated “my request is for "a copy draft Sectoral Plan that was submitted to the Department of Housing as stated in the decision." The request is clearly for a copy of a specific draft that was submitted to another public authority. That specific draft cannot possibly be in the course of completion. The submitted draft was complete once it left the realm of DAFM. DAFM considered the draft sufficiently complete to submit it to DHLGH.... There is a measure of contradiction in DAFM's responses. In 25 112 "the draft Sectoral Plan was submitted to the Department of Housing, Local Government & Heritage (DHLGH)" the IR decision is trying to portray this as a "rough draft copy of the plan". My request is clearly for a draft. Any draft document should be appropriately identified. Release would not be misleading as it should be clear that what was provided to DHLGH by DAFM was a draft. Without prejudice to my contention the Article 9(2)(c) does not apply; The application of Article 10(3) is generic and has not considered the public interest in the release of the specific information requested. The decision states that Article 10(5) has been considered but does not explain how.”
7. On 2 January 2026, the Department contacted the appellant to inform him that “The Sectoral Action Work Plans have now been published by the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage. Details of all plans, including the Forestry Plan, can be found here
:
Sectoral Action Work Plans
.”
8. The OCEI Investigator in this case then engaged with the appellant to find out if the information published satisfied his original AIE request and his appeal could be settled informally. The appellant wished to continue with his appeal on the basis that he had requested the draft action plan.
9. On 20 February 2026 the Department emailed the appellant a copy of the draft sectoral plan as submitted to the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage which was the subject of this AIE request. The appellant responded that “The document was submitted in May 2025 - can you explain why you are releasing it to me now - months after I sought it?”
10. The OCEI Investigator did not contact the appellant following release of the draft action plan as the appellant had then stated that he had chosen to withdraw from informal communication with this Office in relation to informal resolution of his appeals.
Article 15(5)
11. Article 15(5) of the AIE Regulations states: “The Commissioner may deem an appeal to be withdrawn if the public authority makes the requested information available, in whole or in part, prior to a formal decision of the Commissioner under article 12(5). In such circumstances, the Commissioner may waive or refund all or part of the appeal fee.”
12. As I have set out in previous decisions, this Office is committed to playing our role in enabling timely and appropriate access to information on the environment. In doing so I must recognise that the resources of public authorities are not unlimited. Neither are the resources of this Office. Therefore, I believe the best way to achieve appropriate access to environmental information is to focus the resources available to requesters, public bodies and this office on ensuring the release of information which should be released rather than expending resources on cases where the information has already been released.
13. In this case I am satisfied that the Department has now released all information within scope of the original AIE request and having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I deem this appeal to be withdrawn as per article 15(5) of the AIE Regulations.
Appeal to the High Court
14. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Ger Deering
Commissioner for Environmental Information
respondent: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine

title: Ms. H & AirNav Ireland
text:
Decision
Ms. H & AirNav Ireland
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-163101-Y7J7V5
Published on 16 June 2026
Context
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether the information requested by the appellant is “environmental information” within the meaning of the definition of article 3(1) of the AIE regulations.
16 June 2026
Context
R116 Air Accident
1. As detailed in the Air Accident Investigation Unit Report (‘AAIU’) final report, on March 14, 2017, a Sikorsky S-92A helicopter, registration EI-ICR (call sign Rescue 116), which was being operated by a private operator on behalf of the Irish Coast Guard, was en route from Dublin to Blacksod, Co. Mayo. It was the Flight Crew’s intention was to refuel at Blacksod before proceeding, as tasked, to provide Top Cover for another of the Operator’s helicopters, which had been tasked to airlift a casualty from a fishing vessel, situated approximately 140 nautical miles off the west coast of Ireland. At 00.46 hrs while positioning for an approach to Blacksod from the west, the Helicopter, which was flying at 200 feet above the sea, collided with terrain at the western end of Black Rock, departed from controlled flight, and impacted with the sea, resulting in the tragic loss of all four crew members. The appellant’s request for information under the AIE Regulations is related to this air accident.
The relevant Public Authority
2. The appellant made her original request to the Irish Aviation Authority (‘IAA’) on the 17 May 2022. As confirmed by AirNav Ireland, the air navigation services functions of the IAA moved to AirNav Ireland on 30 April 2023. Therefore, it is necessary to outline this restructuring within the IAA as it relates to the appellant’s AIE request.
3. On review of the IAA’s website, it is described as a commercial semi-state company and the single civil aviation regulator for Ireland. The IAA is responsible for the regulation of safety, security and consumer interests.
4. According to the IAA’s annual report 2024, the Air Navigation and Transport Act 2022 provided for the restructuring of Ireland’s civil aviation regulatory framework to ensure compliance with international best practice. The Act provided for the merger of the safety and security regulation functions of the IAA with the economic and consumer protection functions of the Commission for Aviation Regulation, within IAA, to create a single civil aviation regulator. It also provided for the air navigation functions of the IAA to transfer to a separate commercial, semi-state company, the Irish Air Navigation Service DAC trading as AirNav Ireland. This merger and separation formally took place on 01 May 2023.
5. As the appellant’s current appeal to this Office is post this restructure, her appeal is being processed by AirNav Ireland as the public authority now holding the relevant records.
Background
6. On 17 May 2022 the appellant made the following request to the IAA under the AIE Regulations:
a. “A copy of the report prepared by the Air Traffic Controllers on the R116 crash at Blacksod Bay in March 2017. I am requesting a copy of this report under the Access to Information on the environment regulations on the basis to see what role environmental factors such as weather conditions, geographic location, air traffic conditions etc., contributed to this accident.
b. I am also requesting all written correspondence including e-mails, faxes, letters, memos, text messages including those on social messaging apps such as Whatsapp, to do with this report and its findings under the same regulations.”
7. On 17 July 2022 the IAA responded by furnishing the appellant with a report and stated that the requested information was included in this report.
8. On 26 July 2022, the appellant requested an internal review. The appellant submitted that the report that issued was the final IAA report and not the Air Traffic Controller’s report as requested.
9. On 25 August 2022, the IAA replied to the appellant affirming the original decision on the basis that operational data is protected under regulation 376/2014. Regulation 376 of 2014 is a European Union Regulation concerning the reporting, analysis and follow up of occurrences in civil aviation. The IAA confirmed that the AAIU is the competent authority for the State and that it is the appropriate body from which any such information should be requested.
10. The appellant brought an appeal to this Office on 30 August 2022.
11. In the decision on that appeal
OCE-127739-F6N9X8
dated 30 November 2023, the Commissioner found that the request had not been dealt with in accordance with Articles 3(4) and 4(5) of the Directive, stated that the IAA must comply with the AIE Regulations and advised it to immediately put in place appropriate measures to ensure proper engagement with requesters and with this Office in relation to AIE appeals.
12. The Commissioner annulled the IAA’s decision and remitted the matter for fresh consideration by the IAA with the expectation that the fresh decision-making progress would culminate in a decision which complies with the requirements of the AIE Regulations and the AIE Directive.
13. Following this decision, a new internal review decision does not appear to have been issued to the appellant. As a result, the appellant was obliged to contact AirNav (post the restructure) on the 24 July 2025, requesting this new internal review, some twenty months later.
14. On the 15 September 2025, AirNav Ireland issued a new internal review decision to the appellant in which it identified two records falling within the scope of the appellant’s request, it confirmed that refusal to release these records was based on articles 8(a)(iv) and 9(1)(b) of the AIE regulations. I note there was a delay to the statutory timeframes here, this appears to have occurred around the same time that IAA underwent a significant restructure, as I have set out above.
15. The appellant brought an appeal to this Office on 01 October 2025. The appellant in her appeal sought a review of the internal review of 15 September 2025 on the following basis:
“AirNav are refusing to release information sought on the basis that to do so would:
1) Adversely affect confidentiality.
2) A High Court Order is required.
3) Would impact the course of justice and criminal inquiries.
4) The public interest of releasing is outweighed by the public interest of withholding.
However, there are no on-going criminal inquiries or investigations. The final report has been completed and its findings were published four years ago in November 2021. In addition, when this final report was released voice recordings of those on board were broadcasted on the national television even though a High Court order was neither sought nor granted.
The R116 crash is regarded as the worse aviation accident involving a search and rescue team in the country's history. Two bodies were recovered and the bodies of two others have yet to be recovered. So given all of the reasons cited above by me the public interest in releasing this information far outweighs the public interest of not doing so."
16. I am directed by the Commissioner for Environmental Information to carry out a review of this appeal. I have now completed this review under article 12(5) of the Regulations. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by the appellant and by the Department. In addition, I have had regard to:
• the Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (the Minister’s Guidance);
• Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
• the 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention); and
• The Aarhus Convention—An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (‘the Aarhus Guide’).
• The judgments of the Superior Courts in Redmond & Anor v Commissioner for Environmental Information & Anor [2020] IECA 83 (Redmond), Electricity Supply Board v Commissioner for Environmental Information & Lar Mc Kenna [2020] IEHC 190 (ESB) and Right to Know v Commissioner for Environmental Information & RTÉ [2021] IEHC 353 (RTÉ).
• The judgment of the Court of Appeal of England and Wales in Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy v Information Commissioner and Henney [2017] EWCA Civ 844 (Henney) which is referenced in the decisions in Redmond, ESB and RTÉ; and
• The decisions of the Court of Justice of the European Union in C-321/96 Wilhelm Mecklenburg v Kreis Pinneberg - Der Landrat (Mecklenburg), and C-316/01 Eva Glawischnig v Bundesminister für soziale Sicherheit und Generationen (Glawischnig).
• The judgment of the Court of Appeal in Electricity Supply Board -v- Commissioner for Environmental Information [2026] IECA 57.
17. What follows does not comment or make findings on each and every argument advanced, but all relevant points have been considered.
Scope of Review
18. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, my role is to review the public authority’s internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it. Where appropriate in the circumstances of an appeal, I will require the public authority to make available environmental information to the appellant.
19. My powers as Commissioner for Environmental information apply only in respect of environmental information held by or for the public authority and the matter of whether the information sought is “environmental information” is a threshold jurisdictional question. I am cognisant that in my previous decision in respect of this request for information,
OCE-127739-F6N9X8
dated 30 November 2023, that the issue as to whether the information sought in the appellant’s request was environmental information pursuant to 3(1) of the AIE Regulations did not arise, and it was therefore not addressed in the decision.
20. A review by this Office is considered to be de novo, which means that it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of this decision. This approach has been endorsed by the decision of the High Court in M50 Skip Hire Recycling Limited v the Commissioner for Environmental Information 2020 IEHC 430. Further it is clear from the comments of the Court of Appeal in Redmond, at paragraph 51, that the nature of a review by this Office is inquisitorial, rather than adversarial in nature. The extent of the inquiry is determined by this Office, and not by the parties to the appeal.
21. In this regard, given the de novo nature of reviews conducted by this Office, I am satisfied that it appropriate in this appeal to focus on the matter of whether the information sought is “environmental information” such that it falls within the remit of article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations.
22. If it is determined that the subject information does fall within 3(1) then it will be necessary to address AirNav Ireland’s refusal to release the records based on articles 8(a)(iv) and 9(1)(b) of the AIE regulations. However, if it is determined that the information subject of the appeal is not considered to be environmental information in accordance with article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations then that is the end of the matter, as I only have the power to make an assessment of the application of articles 8(a)(iv) and 9(1)(b) of the AIE regulations by AirNav Ireland in respect of “environmental information.”
Analysis and Findings
Position of the parties
23. In a submission to this Office dated 30 April 2026, Air Nav stated the following in respect of article 3(1), “AirNav Ireland notes the provisions of Article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations and the associated case law. AirNav Ireland is of the view that the information sought under the request is not environmental information within the meaning of Article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations.”
24. In response to the investigators preliminary view and AirNav Ireland’s submission, the appellant in a submission dated 14 May 2026 stated, “I do not agree with that view, and I am asking that the Commissioner finds that the records requested; or at least parts of them; do fall within article 3(1) of the said Regulations.” The appellant’s arguments included but were not limited to the following points.
25. The appellant stated that her request relates to “a report prepared by Air Traffic Controllers into the R116 crash at Blacksod Bay in March 2017, along with all related written communications (including emails, messages, memos, etc.) about that report and its findings and it this is not just about a past aviation incident; it’s about how that incident was reviewed and discussed by air traffic control personnel”.
26. The appellant confirmed acceptance that “the key issue is whether the material qualifies as “environmental information” under article 3(1), and that there must be more than a minimal link to the environment. However, the case law also makes clear that the definition is broad, and information does not have to be purely environmental in nature to come within scope.”
27. The appellant submitted that the “real question is whether the content of the records fits within one or more of the categories in article 3(1), rather than how the records might be labelled in general terms. In my view, the records clearly have the potential to fall within article 3(1)(c), which covers information on measures or activities affecting, or likely to affect, environmental elements” and in her view “a report by Air Traffic Controllers into a helicopter crash, along with related communications, is capable of including information about air navigation, air traffic control, aviation safety, operational procedures, emergency response, and accident prevention. These are regulated public safety activities that operate within the air and atmosphere, and in this case relate directly to an incident at a coastal location”.
28. The appellant submitted that the information requested potentially falls under article 3(1)(a), (b), (c) and/or (f) as follows:
“If the report or correspondence deals with matters like routing, communications, weather, visibility, marine conditions, emergency response, or lessons learned, then those parts of the records are clearly about activities or measures within article 3(1)(c). Similarly, the records may fall within article 3(1)(f), which covers human health and safety where it is affected by environmental factors or related activities. The R116 crash involved loss of life in a coastal/marine environment. Any reasonable analysis of safety, conditions, or operational response is capable of engaging article 3(1)(f).
It would be too narrow to treat this provision as limited to pollution or public health scenarios only. Article 3(1)(a) is also relevant, as it includes environmental elements such as air, atmosphere, water, and coastal and marine areas. Given that the crash occurred at Blacksod Bay, any discussion of weather, visibility, terrain, or marine conditions would surely fall within this category.
Likewise, article 3(1)(b) may be engaged if the records refer to fuel, debris, emissions, noise, or any other releases, including human remains into the environment arising from the crash or recovery operations. Whether this applies will depend on the content, which is why a detailed assessment of the records is important. The broader aviation law context supports this approach.
Air traffic control and aviation safety functions are part of a regulated public safety system, and accident review processes are aimed at preventing future incidents. This reinforces the view that these are “measures or activities” within the meaning of article 3(1)(c). I am not suggesting that every aviation-related record is environmental information. But records relating to the review of a helicopter crash in a coastal setting are clearly capable of falling within scope, depending on what they contain.
In that context, AirNav Ireland’s position; as outlined in your letter; seems far too conclusory. It doesn’t explain, by reference to the actual contents of the records, nor why they would not fall within any part of article 3(1). A broad general assertion that they are not environmental information simply is not sufficient in circumstances like this.”
29. The appellant further submitted as her request “covers multiple records, not just a single document. Some parts may fall within the definition even if others do not. For this reason, I ask that the records are considered individually, or at least on a part-by-part basis, rather than as a single category.”
30. The appellant asked that “the Commissioner not to adopt the preliminary view that the requested information falls outside article 3(1). Instead, I ask that it be found that the records - or relevant parts of them - fall within article 3(1)(a), (b), (c) and/or (f), particularly as information relating to aviation safety, air navigation, operational review, and accident prevention. If that conclusion cannot be reached for all of the material, I request that the records be assessed in detail and that any parts falling within the definition be identified accordingly.”
31. Finally, the appellant stated that “RTÉ’s Prime Time special on the Rescue 116 crash, broadcast on 5 November 2021, the night before the AAIU final report was published, played actual transmissions between the helicopter and Dublin Air Traffic Control”.
Definition of Environmental Information
32. Article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations is the relevant provision to consider where the issue is whether information is "environmental information". In line with Article 2(1) of the AIE Directive, article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations provides that "environmental information" means:
“any information in written, visual, aural, electronic or any other material form on —
(a) the state of the elements of the environment, such as air and atmosphere, water, soil, land, landscape and natural sites including wetlands, coastal and marine areas, biological diversity and its components, including genetically modified organisms and the interaction among these elements,
(b) factors, such as substances, energy, noise, radiation or waste, including radioactive waste, emissions, discharges and other releases into the environment, affecting or likely to affect the elements of the environment
(c) measures (including administrative measures), such as policies, legislation, plans, programmes, environmental agreements, and activities affecting or likely to affect the elements and factors referred to in paragraphs (a) and (b) as well as measures or activities designed to protect those elements,
(d) reports on the implementation of environmental legislation,
(e) cost-benefit and other economic analyses and assumptions used within the framework of the measures and activities referred to in paragraph (c), and
(f) the state of human health and safety, including the contamination of the food chain, where relevant, conditions of human life, cultural sites and built structures inasmuch as they are, or may be, affected by the state of the elements of the environment referred to in paragraph (a) or, through those elements, by any of the matters referred to in paragraphs (b) and (c).”
33. The right of access under the AIE Regulations is to information “on” one or more of the six categories at (a)to (f) of the definition. According to national and EU case law on the definition of “environmental information”, while the concept of “environmental information as defined in the AIE Directive is broad (Mecklenburg at paragraph 19), there must be more than a minimal connection with the environment (Glawisching at paragraph 25). Information does not have to be intrinsically environmental to fall within the scope of the definition (Redmond at paragraph 58; see also ESB at paragraph 43). However, a mere connection of link to the environment is not sufficient to bring information within the definition of environmental information. Otherwise, the scope of the definition would be unlimited in a manner that would be contrary to the judgments of the Court of Appeal and the CJEU.
Identification of a measure or activity
34. Paragraph (c) requires the identification of a relevant measure or activity, which the information sought is “on”.
35. When identifying a measure, it is useful to draw on the relevant case law. Information may be “on” more than one measure or activity ( Henney
at paragraph 42). The Irish Court of Appeal in ESB (paragraph 76) referred to Henney
, where Beatson L.J. accepted that it was permissible to look beyond the precise issue with which the information is concerned (which in this case is the Air Traffic Controllers investigation report into the R116 air crash) to identify the measure, but not to look at issues with which the information is not concerned or with which it is merely connected (para. 39). He did not go so far as to require that the information be “directly or immediately concerned”
with the measure so as to exclude consideration of the broader context. He stated (at para. 43 of the judgment):
“It follows that identifying the measure that the disputed information ‘on’ may require consideration of the wider context, and is not strictly limited to the precise issue with which the information is concerned, here the communications and data component, or the document containing the information, here the Project Assessment Review. It may be relevant to consider the purpose for which the information was produced, how important the information is to that purpose, how it is to be used and whether access to it would enable the public to be informed about, or to participate in, decision-making in a better way. None of these matters may be apparent on the face of the information itself. It was not in dispute that, when identifying the measure, a tribunal should apply the definition in the [Regulations] purposively, bearing in mind the modern approach to the interpretation of legislation, and particularly to international and European measures such as the Aarhus Convention and the Directive. It is then necessary to consider whether the measure so identified has the requisite environmental impact for the purposes of regulation 2(1).”
36. The Irish Courts have made clear that when identifying the relevant measure or activity, one may consider the wider context and is not strictly limited to the precise issue with which the information is concerned (ESB No. 1 at paragraph 43). Further, the list of examples of measures and activities given at paragraph (c) is not exhaustive, but it contains illustrative examples (Redmond at paragraph 55). The Court of Justice of the European Union (‘CJEU’) stated in Mecklenburg that the term ‘measure’ serves “merely to make it clear that the acts governed by the directive included all forms of administrative activity” (Mecklenburg at paragraph 20), and the Irish Courts adopted a similarly expansive approach should be taken to the term ‘activity’ (RTÉ at paragraph 19).
37. In my opinion the most appropriate and relevant measure here in respect of the request is the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident. This is the case in respect of both parts of the appellant’s AIE request, which are clearly interrelated.
38. The records subject to this review are identified by AirNav Ireland as the “Safety Management Unit's Report” and a “Partial transcript of Shannon Air Traffic Control to aircraft R116”. AirNav Ireland submitted by way of explanation that the Safety Management Unit's Report “constitutes opinion expressed in the analysis of information, including CVR and FDR information, by the safety management unit of the IAA when carrying out an investigation into the accident involving aircraft callsign R116” (CVR being Cockpit Voice recordings and FDR being Flight Deck Recordings) and that “Partial transcript of Shannon Air Traffic Control to aircraft R116” “constitutes a transcript of a recording from an air traffic control unit.”
39. Both records relate to the R116 air accident and are incident specific operational and communicative records, created for safety and operational purposes. I am of the view that the overarching measure to which both of these records relate is the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident.
40. In my view, paragraph (c) of the definition of environmental information provided for in article 3(1) of the Regulations, which provides that environmental information” means any information on “measures (including administrative measures), such as policies, legislation, plans, programmes, environmental agreements, and activities affecting or likely to affect the elements and factors referred to in paragraphs (a) and (b) as well as measures or activities designed to protect those elements, is the only paragraph relevant to this review.
41. The next issue to be considered is whether the measure, in this case the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident, affects or is likely to affect or designed to protect the environment.
Whether the measure or activity is affecting, likely to affect or designed to protect the environment
42. A measure or activity is “likely to affect” the elements and factors of the environment if there is a real and substantial possibility that it will affect the environment, whether directly or indirectly. Collins J, delivering judgment on behalf of the Court of Appeal in Redmond, noted that “63. Drawing together these statements, it appears to me that, for the purposes of paragraph (c), a measure or activity is “likely to affect” the environment if there is a real and substantial possibility that it will affect the environment, whether directly or indirectly. Something more than a remote or theoretical possibility is required (because that would sweep too widely and could result in the “general and unlimited right of access” that Glawischnig indicates the AIE Directive was not intended to provide) but it is not necessary to establish the probability of a relevant environmental impact (because that would, in my opinion, sweep too narrowly and risk undermining the fundamental objectives of the AIE Directive)
.(emphasis added)”
43. The Court of Appeal in ESB gave its interpretation of Redmond at paragraph 87: “Redmond concerned a request for access to information regarding the sale of forestry land by Coillte Teoranta. In considering whether the information was environmental information, the Commissioner, and consequently the court, focused on whether the sale of land was a “measure affecting or likely to affect” the environment within the meaning of Article 3(1)(c). In that context Collins J. held that although a sale of land will not of itself result in any alteration to the land, it can nonetheless constitute a “measure” where there is evidence the purchaser intends to develop the land, even where such development would be subject to obtaining development consent. The test for whether the measure is likely to affect the environment is whether there is a real and substantial possibility it will affect the environment, whether directly or indirectly. A possibility must be more than remote or theoretical but need not amount to a probability that environmental impact will occur.”
44. It is clear that in order to determine whether the measure, is likely to affect the environment I must be persuaded there is a real and substantial possibility it will affect the environment, whether directly or indirectly. Accordingly, I have carefully considered the purpose of the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident. In this regard, I have considered the detail AirNav have provided around such investigations generally. I have also considered the records it has provided me with in relation to this case specifically. These records include the IAA Safety Management Unit report into the R116 accident, and a partial transcript of Shannon Air Traffic Control to aircraft R116.
45. I consider that these records were utilised to establish the facts of what occurred in the lead up to the accident R116 air accident. I note that the AAIU as part of its investigation into the R116 air accident had access to both records, and aspects of these records were incorporated into the AAIU’s published final report. The purpose of the AAIU’s final report was to establish what happened, identify the causes and contributing factors and make safety recommendations to prevent similar air accidents in the future.
46. I have outlined the position of the parties in detail above. I have had regard to the decision and submission of AirNav Ireland, the information in the records subject to this appeal and the appellant’s submissions to this Office.
47. I note the appellant’s contention that the “real question is whether the content of the records fits within one or more of the categories in article 3(1), rather than how the records might be labelled in general terms”
and in her view that “the records clearly have the potential to fall within article 3(1)(c), which covers information on measures or activities affecting, or likely to affect, environmental elements”
.
48. As I have already set out, the test I need to be satisfied of is whether the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident is a measure affecting or likely to affect the environment as it is the “measure”, not the information “on” that measure, that is subject to that threshold test (Redmond at paragraph 57). It is my view; there is no real and substantial possibility that the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident, as a measure, is likely to affect the environment in the manner described in paragraph (c).
49. I consider that the connection between the measure, and any consequent effect on the environment to be overly remote and at best minimal and tenuous. It is important to reiterate, as it relates to the circumstances of this case, that there must be more than a minimal connection with the environment (Glawisching at paragraph 25) a mere connection of link to the environment is not sufficient to bring information within the definition of environmental information. Having carefully considered all submissions, I have not seen any evidence to persuade me of such a link.
50. I am not persuaded that the test as set out by the Court of Appeal in Redmond, that there is a real and substantial possibility that it will affect the environment, is met, even indirectly. The examples that the appellant has provided are, to my mind, too far removed to be considered anything more than a remote or theoretical possibility of effecting the environment. To find otherwise would plainly expand the scope of AIE in a manner that would be in direct contradiction to the judgments of the national courts and the CJEU, which have clearly determined that the scope of the definition of environmental information is broad but not unlimited, as referenced above.
Whether the information is on the measure or activity
51. Where the relevant measure or activity has the requisite environmental effect, one must consider whether the requested information is “on” that measure or activity within the meaning of article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations. In this case, having found that the relevant measure and/or activity i.e. the Air Traffic Controllers Report into the R116 air accident does not have the requisite environmental effect, it is not necessary for me to consider whether the requested information is “on” that measure or activity within the meaning of article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations.
52. I note the appellant in her submissions to this Office put forth several suggestions as to how the records - or relevant parts of them - fall within article 3(1)(a), (b), (c) and/or (f) (see paragraph 28). The final step to consider is whether the information requested by the appellant is information “on” the state of the elements of the environment and the factors likely to affect these elements.
53. The word “on” has been the subject of considerable litigation in the context of Article 3(1)(c). But there is nothing in those cases that limits their findings to the meaning of “on” in the context of paragraph (c) only and in my view the principles outlined in Henney are equally applicable to all of the paragraphs in the definition of environmental information.
54. The Court in Henney found that “information is ‘on’ a measure if it is about, relates to or concerns the measure in question (paragraph 37).” It is not sufficient for information to be merely connected to the measure or activity, but the information need not to be specifically, directly or immediately about the measure or activity.
55. In support of this conclusion, Henney further suggests that, in determining whether information is “on”
the relevant measure or activity, it may be relevant to consider the purpose of the information such as why it was produced, how important it is to that purpose, how it is to be used, and whether access to it advances the purposes of the Aarhus Convention and the AIE Directive (paragraph 43; see also ESB, paragraph 42). Information that does not advance the purposes of the Aarhus Convention and the AIE Directive may not be “on” the relevant measure or activity (Redmond, paragraph 99).
56. As the Court noted in Henney, the recitals of both the Aarhus Convention and the AIE Directive refer to the requirement that citizens have access to information to provide for a greater awareness of environmental matters, to enable more effective participation by the public in environmental decision-making and to facilitate the free exchange of views with the aim that all of this should lead, ultimately, to a better environment. Those recitals give an indication of how the very broad language of the text of the provisions in the Convention and Directive may have to be assessed and provide a framework for determining the question of whether information is on a particular measure. Finally, as the High Court noted in ESB information that is integral to a measure or activity is information “on” it while information that is too remote from the relevant measure or activity does not qualify as environmental information (ESB, paragraphs 38, 40, 41 and 43).
57. Taking in to account the specific facts and context of this appeal and having reviewed the records, I am of the view that the information is not environmental information as it is too remote without a real and substantial possibility that it will affect the elements and factors referred to in article 3(1)(a) and (b), directly or indirectly.
58. I have considered the examples provided by the appellant in support of her contention that the information could be capable of affecting the environment pursuant to article 3(1)(a) and (b). However, nothing in the appellant’s submissions or evident from the information before this Office has persuaded me that these suggestions amount to more than a theoretical link.
59. In light of the Courts commentary regarding the Aarhus Convention and the AIE Directive I have considered if citizens would be better informed and more able to contribute to environmental decision-making if they were able to access the information subject to this appeal. It is my view, that in the circumstances of this specific appeal, this would not be the case, and releasing the records would not serve to advance the aims of the Aarhus Convention and AIE Directive.
60. Accordingly, as I have found the definition of environmental information under article 3(1) has not been met, therefore an assessment of the exemptions applied by AirNav Ireland in support of its refusal of the appellant’s request i.e. articles 8(a)(iv) and 9(1)(b) of the AIE regulations, is not required in this instance.
61. Finally, the appellant in her appeal to this Office and in submissions dated 14 May 2026, refers to the final report into the R116 air accident having been completed and its findings published four years ago in November 2021. Also, the appellant refers to the “RTÉ’s Prime Time special on the Rescue 116 crash, which was broadcast on 05 November 2021, the night before the AAIU final report was published, and which the appellant contends “played actual transmissions between R116 and the Dublin Air Traffic Control.”
62. As I have determined that the information subject of the appeal is not considered to be environmental information in accordance with article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations, it is not necessary for me to comment on the above.
Decision
63. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I affirm AirNav Ireland’s decision.
Appeal to the High Court
64. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Gemma Farrell
On behalf of the Commissioner for Environmental Information

title: Company X & Dublin City Council
text:
Decision
Company X & Dublin City Council
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-135831-B3F8K9
Published on 12 June 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether the Council has carried out adequate searches pursuant to article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations and whether the Council was justified in withholding relevant information under article 9(1)(b) of the AIE Regulations.
12 June 2026
Background
1. On 17 November 2022, the appellant submitted the following request to the Council:
“[A] [C]opies (in soft copy format) of all records and/or environmental information held and/or under the control of Dublin City Council, its elected members, legal advisors, technical advisors or any of its service providers, in respect of the substantive matter touching on the consideration and making of the Dublin City Development Plan 2022 – 2028 identified below, including (but not limited to) the following:
1. letters;
2. emails;
3. memorandums;
4. typed or handwritten notes of meetings / telephone conversations;
5. minutes of meetings / teleconferences;
6. text or instant messaging, including WhatsApp messages;
7. reports;
8. documents;
9. correspondence (both internal and external); and
10. any drafts of the above items at 1-9. but excluding the following:
all correspondence and materials shared between Company X and Dublin City Council;
• any records or information which attract legal professional privilege; and
• any records or information of a purely logistical or administrative nature e.g. meeting request emails.
This is a request for records and environmental information which substantively relate to: 1. correspondence to or from any elected members in relation to the former St. Paul's Playing Pitches, Raheny, Dublin 5 (St. Pauls);
2. correspondence to or from any elected members relating to motion V3.11: MOT-01969 or motion V3.12: MOT-01960 submitted by Councillor Catherine Stocker; and RA139/004/AC#44573891.1
3. correspondence to or from any elected members relating to the Chief Executive’s recommendation that St. Pauls be zoned Z1 and Z9.”
2. On 20 December 2022, the appellant requested an internal review, as the Council had not issued its decision within the prescribed statutory timeframe.
3. On 23 January 2023, the Council issued its effective position. The Council upheld its previous decision to grant/part grant access to some records and refuse access to other records. It attached a schedule of records. It identified ten documents, which fell within the scope of the appellant’s request. The Council granted access to records 1, 2, (b), 7, 8 and 10; part-granted access to records 4 and 4(a) and it refused access to records 3, 5, 6 and 9.
4. The appellant submitted an appeal to my Office on 23 February 2023.
5. I am directed by the Commissioner for Environmental Information to carry out a review of this appeal. I have now completed this review under article 12(5) of the Regulations. In so doing, I have had regard to all submissions made by the parties. I have also reviewed the records at issue. In addition, I have had regard to:
a. the Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (the Minister’s Guidance);
b. Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
c. the 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention); and
d. The Aarhus Convention—An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (‘the Aarhus Guide’).
6. What follows does not comment or make findings on each and every argument advanced, but all relevant points have been considered.
Scope of Review
7. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, my role is to review the public authority’s internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it. Where appropriate in the circumstances of an appeal, I will require the public authority to make available environmental information to the appellant.
8. The scope of this review is concerned with whether the Council has carried out adequate pursuant to article 7(5) and whether the Council was justified in refusing access to the appellant’s request for information under article 9(1)b) of the AIE Regulations.
Preliminary Matters
9. While the Council relied on both article 8(a)(iv) and article 9(1)(b) to justify refusal, it is my view that protection for legal professional privilege most appropriately falls within the exception in article 9(1)(b) of the AIE Regulations. Legal professional privilege is a key tenet of the administration of justice is relevant to article 9(1)(b) of the AIE Regulations. Accordingly, for the purpose of this review, I will examine whether the Council is justified in withholding information under the exemption article 9(1)(b) of the AIE Regulations.
Analysis and Findings
Article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations
10. Article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations is the relevant provision to consider, where the question arises as to whether the requested environmental information or any further environmental information is held by, or for, the public authority concerned. It provides as follows:
“Where a request is made to a public authority and the information requested is not held by or for the authority concerned, that authority shall inform the applicant as soon as possible that the information is not held by or for it.”
11. What will be considered reasonable will vary from case to case, but as a general guide, I set out below the type of information that my Office would generally expect to be set out in a decision where a public authority is relying on article 7(5) of the Regulations:
i. an outline of exactly which areas/units etc. of the organisation were searched for the information.
ii. an explanation of how searches were carried out (i.e. manually, by computer, by name, by key words). Keywords should be recorded and provided in the decision as appropriate.
iii. details of the individuals consulted in connection with the search.
iv. a description of the searches carried out to cover the possibility of misfiled/misplaced records.
v. details of guidelines, practices, procedures and arrangements in relation to the storage, filing, archiving, retention and destruction of the type of information requested in this case.
vi. the basis on which the public authority has concluded that it does not hold any information within the scope of the appellant’s request and that no such information is held by any other person or body on its behalf.
12. In this case the appellant is not satisfied that the Council have conducted adequate searches pertaining to all information falling within the scope of the request.
13. In a submission dated 22 May 2026, the Council stated that in its decision, it identified and granted the appellant with access to the following records:
“Record 1
Email from the Chief Executive to Councillors dated 18th May 2018.
Record 2
Emails from Planning Officer to the Law Agent and the City Planner including submissions and 10 separate attachments.
Attachment 1- Raheny GAA
Attachment 2 - Raheny United Football Club
Attachment 3 - Geese to the rescue by Michael Smith dated 05/02/2018
Attachment 4 - An Taisce submission dated 05/02/2018
Attachment 5 - Birdwatch Ireland dated 05/02/2018
Attachment 6 - Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht dated 05/02/2018
Attachment 7 - Peter Sweetman & Associates
Attachment 8 – Clontarf Football Club
Attachment 9 – MacCabe Durney Barnes
Attachment 10 – Clontarf GAA Club
Record 7
Emails from Councillor to Assistant Chief Executive in advance of November Council Meeting
Record 8
Email from Councillor to City Planning Officer referencing replies to NCAC Council Questions 23 and 24 dated 15th November 2021.”
14. The Council further provided this Office with a detailed response of the searches, which had been undertaken. Upon receipt of the request, the Council stated that it searched its “Planning Shared drive, City Planners email account. Planning Consultation Portal, Personal folders, hard files/folders, Office.”
The Council highlighted that it applied the search keywords “Marlet, St. Paul’s, St. Paul’s Playing Pitches, motion V3.11, Mot-01969, motion V3.12: MOT-01960, Cllr Catherine Stocker”
. Having undertaken its searches, the Council confirmed that it granted the appellant with access to records 1, 2, 7 and 8; part-granted access to records 4 and 4(a) and it refused access to records 3, 5, 6 and 9.
15. I note that the Regulations do not require absolute certainty as to the existence or location of records, as situations arise where records are lost or simply cannot be found, or, indeed, may have been destroyed in line with the body’s records management policies. The passage of time is also relevant factor in such appeals. It is also important to note that the Commissioner does not generally expect public authorities to carry out extensive or indefinite general searches for records simply because an applicant asserts that more records should or might exist, or rejects a public authorises explanation of why a record does not exist. The test set out in article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations is whether the public authority has taken all reasonable steps to locate the record(s) sought.
16. Having considered the explanations provided by the Council, I am satisfied that the Council has taken adequate steps to identify and locate all relevant environmental information held by it in this particular case. Accordingly, I find that article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations applies.
Exemptions under the AIE Regulations
17. Articles 8 and 9 of the AIE Regulations provide certain grounds for refusal of information. Both articles must be read alongside article 10 of the AIE Regulations. Article 10(1) provides that notwithstanding articles 8 and 9(1)(c) of the AIE Regulations, a request for environmental information shall not be refused where the request relates to information on emissions into the environment. Article 10(3) requires a public authority to consider each request on an individual basis and weigh the public interest served by disclosure against the interest served by refusal. Article 10(4) provides that the grounds for refusal of a request shall be interpreted on a restrictive basis having regard to the public interest served by disclosure. Article 10(5) provides that nothing in articles 8 or 9 shall authorise a public authority not to make available environmental information which, although held with information to which article 8 or 9 relates, may be separated from such information.
18. When relying on articles 8 or 9 of the AIE Regulations a public authority must demonstrate a clear link between disclosure of the specific information that it has withheld and any adverse effect. It must set out the reasons why it considers that the disclosure of the information at issue could specifically and actually undermine the interest protected by the exceptions relied upon, as set out by the CJEU at paragraph 69 of Land Baden-Wurttemberg v DR
, Case C-619/19. This sets a high threshold as the risk must be reasonably foreseeable and not purely hypothetical. A mere assertion of an expectation of harm is not sufficient.
Article 9(1)(b) of the AIE Regulations
19. Article 9(1)(b) seeks to implement Article 4(2)(c) of the AIE Directive, which is in turn based on Article 4(4)(c) of the Aarhus Convention. I note that the Aarhus Guide takes a narrow approach to construction of the relevant provision in the Aarhus Convention, interpreting “the course of justice”
as referring to “active proceedings within the courts”. However, I also note that the Aarhus Guide, while a source of helpful guidance, is but a Guide, is not legally binding and is not determinative ( Right to Know CLG v Commissioner for Environmental Information IEHC 353 , paragraph 20).
20. Legal professional privilege (LPP) is a right of a person to refuse to disclose any communications with his or her lawyer made for the purpose of giving or receiving legal advice. It is a common law right with a constitutional foundation, as a dimension of the protection of the administration of justice afforded by Article 34 of the Irish Constitution. The existence of LPP is predicated on there being a public interest requirement for it in the proper conduct of the administration of justice, such that it is “a fundamental condition on which the administration of justice as a whole rests”
(see Martin v Legal Aid Board [ 2007 IEHC 76 ] and Miley v Flood [ 2001 IEHC 9 ]). In light of this, I accept that the disclosure of information which would breach LPP would, as a result, adversely affect the course of justice, within the meaning of Article 9(1)(b) of the AIE Regulations.
21. LPP encompasses legal advice privilege and litigation privilege. Legal advice privilege covers a communication between “a person and his lawyer acting for him as a lawyer for the purpose of obtaining from such lawyer legal advice whether at the instigation of the client or the lawyer”
(Smurfit Paribas Bank Limited v. AAB Export Finance Limited [1990] 1 IR 469). In light of the guidance set out in McMahon v Irish Aviation Authority 2016 IEHC 221
, I understand that for legal advice privilege to apply:
(a) there must be a communication between a client and a lawyer (including solicitors, barristers, salaried in-house legal advisers, foreign lawyers and the Attorney General);
(b) the communication must have been made in confidence;
(c) the communication must have been made during the course of a professional legal relationship; and
(d) the communication must have been made for the purposes of the giving or receiving of legal advice.
Information withheld on the basis of legal professional privilege (LPP)
22. The Council in its submission to this Office said that “the records under consideration consist of correspondence seeking legal advice, as exchanged between a solicitor and client”
.
Does the exception in article 9(1)(b) apply?
23. In this case, the appellant noted that it is unsatisfactory that the Council has failed to identify the specific type of privilege it is seeking to claim, in circumstances where the burden of proof is entirety upon the party asserting privilege. Furthermore, the appellant submits that the Council has not confirmed whether it is relying on legal advice privilege specifically in respect of the documents which have been refused and notes that the Council has only referred to the umbrella general term privilege.
24. In its submissions, the Council has set out that the records under consideration consist of correspondence seeking legal advice as exchanged between a solicitor and client i.e. legal advice sought and received by the Council from its professional legal advisers together with associated information.
Legal Advice Privilege - Records 3, 6 and 6(a)
25. Legal Advice Privilege only extends to protect communications that contain legal advice as to a person’s rights and liabilities and does not apply to the provision of legal assistance (Smurfit Paribas Bank Ltd v AAB Export Finance Ltd
[1990] 1 IR 469) which includes for example the drafting of contracts or documents. The Commissioner takes the view that correspondence which is of an administrative nature and is not seeking or giving advice is not privileged.
26. In respect of the argument put forward by the appellant in terms of the of the legal advisor acting in his/her professional capacity, provided the prerequisites of advice privilege or litigation privilege are present, the fact that a professional legal adviser is employed as an in-house legal adviser does not prevent the client from asserting privilege over the communications at issue. Moreover, the Commissioner takes the view that advice privilege attaches to records that form part of a continuum of correspondence that results from the original request for advice.
27. With regard to Record 3
, information is sought from the in-house legal advisor on the status of the relevant proceedings at the time. Having regard to the definition of “legal advice” set out above, I am not satisfied that Record 3
constitutes a request for legal advice. The legal adviser, while acting in her capacity as such provided an update on proceedings, despite the fact that the knowledge of the status of the proceedings might have an impact on the options available to the requester, this has no bearing on the fact that the advisor was not actually providing advice as to the liabilities or rights of the client. It is also not clear that the communication arises out of a continuum or original request for advice. Accordingly, I do not consider that Record 3 meets the threshold for legal advice privilege in the circumstances.
28. On the other hand, I am satisfied that -Record 6_ comprises of a confidential communication between the Council’s legal advisor and the Council’s Chief Executive for the purposes of giving advice with respect to potential actions relevant to the proceedings at the time. Accordingly, I find that article 9(1)(b) is applicable in respect of Record 6
. Accordingly, I am of the view that release of the information contained in Record 6 would breach LPP and I am satisfied that the disclosure of this information would adversely affect the course of justice, as it would undermine the general assurance that correspondence with one’s legal advisor will remain confidential. I consider that this applies regardless of whether there are current or envisaged proceedings in place. I acknowledge that LPP does not require related proceedings to be in being. I find therefore, that article 9(1)(b) applies to the information sought.
29. Record 6(a) is an email attachment, which the advice in Record 6 pertains to. More specifically, it is a letter to the Council from the respondents’ representative, a law firm, inviting the Council (a notice party) as directed by the Court to confirm if it is prepared to appear before the Court to discuss if they have anything to contribute at this stage of the proceedings in respect of a certain aspect of the proceedings.
30. Record 6(a) contains no more than a explanation as to what was said in open Court, and what the Court had directed it to do – namely that it would like to hear from the Council on a particular issue. I cannot see how it could be considered to be covered by litigation privilege. Accordingly, I find that article 9(1)(b) is not engaged in respect of Record 6(a).
Litigation Privilege - Records 3, 5, 5(a), 9 and 9(a)
31. For litigation privilege to apply, as set out above, the records must have been created for the dominant purpose of contemplated/pending litigation. In the judgment of the High Court in University College Cork - National University of Ireland v The Electricity Supply Board
([2014] IEHC 135) Finlay Geoghegan J. stated:
"The document must have been created for the dominant purpose of the apprehended or threatened litigation; it is not sufficient that the document has two equal purposes, one of which is apprehended or threatened litigation."
32. As such, a body claiming the exemption must satisfy the Commissioner, on balance, that litigation is contemplated or pending and consideration must be given to the purpose or purposes for which the records were created.
33. The Council has stated that Records 5, 5(a), 9 and 9(a)
were withheld under article 8(a)(iv) (or for the present purposes under article 9(1)(b)) and were created for the purpose of contemplated or pending litigation. As the Commissioner enjoys a broad discretion in relation to the matters to be considered as set out above and given the -de novo_ nature of reviews by this Office, the Commissioner has considered the question of whether Record 3
, which was found not to be privileged on the basis of legal advice, could be exempt from release due to litigation privilege. Following this consideration the Commissioner is satisfied that this is appropriate. Having regard to the contents of the record and is satisfied that it was created for the dominant purpose of pending litigation.
34. The Council have served as a notice party in relation to planning appeals for the above site. The Council has confirmed that it is currently defending a JR case by Raheny 3 Partnership and Raheny GP3 Limited (Record No. 2022/1133 JR) at the High Court; which has now been referred to the Commercial Court. The case in question focusses on the zoning policy for the lands at St. Pauls and also a number of other objectives of the 2022 City Development Plan which impact on their development proposals. The Council acknowledges how there have also been numerous proceedings in relation to the same parcel of lands over a number of years.
35. Record 5
constitutes an email attaching a report created by the City Planning Officer of the Council for the Chief Executive of the Council in respect of an An Bord Pleanála appeal which took place in 2020. The Council have stated that the record relates to a judicial review which was undertaken at the time and that it was created as a result of an emergency motion which urged the involvement of the Council in the matter. It states that while the information withheld by the Council related to proceedings have concluded, it was created solely for the purpose of contemplation of litigation.
36. Record 9
relates to an invitation to the Council to attend judicial review proceedings. The Council confirms that this record comprises of a briefing note prepared for Senior Counsel in advance of a planned hearing. The Council submits that this record was created solely for the purpose of ongoing litigation.
37. Based on the arguments of both the Council and the contents of the records, I accept that litigation was reasonably apprehended at the time the documents in question were brought into being. This however, is not in itself determinative that they are still protected by litigation privilege. Based on my review of the documents, it is clear the Council were preparing to serve as a notice party to the planning permission appeals which An Coimisiún Pleanála [formerly ‘An Bord Pleanála’] and the appellant were involved in.
38. In terms of the arguments concerning the dominant purpose test, it is clear the cover emails were created on foot of potential proceedings that the Council was either anticipating involvement in, or was involved in. The email in Record 3
, the email and attachment in Record 5
and 5(a)
relate directly to the litigation proceedings which were underway at the time. The Commissioner is also satisfied that the attachment was created specifically for that purpose. With respect to -Record 9 and 9(a)_, I find that the briefing note for Senior Counsel was prepared in the context of the High Court proceedings at the time.
39. As stated, the litigation proceedings referred to in the above records have concluded. In order for the duration of litigation privilege to be extended, relevant factors to be considered are whether there are any closely related proceedings currently underway and the identity of the parties to any such litigation. Having considered the records on file, I am satisfied that the Council has satisfied the above requirements in respect of litigation privilege continuing.
The Public Interest test - Records 3, 5, 5(a), 6, 9 and 9(a)
40. The Aarhus Convention recognises that public participation relating to the environment is to be achieved, inter alia
, by making available to members of the public the information necessary to fully so participate. The object of that AIE Directive was to ensure freedom of access to information on the environment held by public authorities in order to ensure that environmental information is progressively made available and disseminated to the public to achieve the widest possible systemic availability.
41. Even where protection from disclosure is identified, either directly or by reference to existing provisions of law, a further step is required. Within Article 4(2)of the Directive it states that:
(a)The grounds for refusal mentioned in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall be interpreted in a restrictive way, taking into account for the particular case the public interest served by disclosure. In every particular case the public interest served by disclosure shall be weighed against the interest served by the refusal.”
42. Articles 10(3) and 10(4) of the AIE Regulations give effect to this provision and state:
(3) The public authority shall consider each request on an individual basis and weigh the public interest served by disclosure against the interest served by refusal.
(4) The grounds for refusal of a request for environmental information shall be interpreted on a restrictive basis having regard to the public interest served by disclosure.
43. There is an important public interest in the disclosure of environmental information as elucidated in the recitals to the AIE Directive. There is a public interest in the openness and transparency of the decision making and enforcement process of Public Authorities in relation to environmental matters. In this case, the Commissioner has examined the requested records and found that they are covered by legal professional privilege as set out above. The importance of LPP has been emphasised in case law including that referenced above and the existence of this privilege has been deemed an essential feature in the administration of justice. The proper administration of justice requires that clients can communicate freely with their legal advisors and third-party experts. There is a strong public and private interest in protecting the proper administration of justice and so in protecting LPP. I find that in this case the public interest in disclosure is not sufficient to outweigh the interest in the Council’s right to LPP in respect of the requested records.
44. Accordingly, I affirm the decision of the Council to refuse access to the requested information contained in Records 3, 5, 5(a), 6, 9 and 9(a)
on the basis that article 9(1)(b) applies to the information by reason of LPP and the interest in refusal outweighs the public interest in disclosure. I do not find that any environmental information can be separated from information to which LPP attaches.
Decision
45. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I vary the Council’s decision as follows: I affirm the Council’s searches for information coming under the scope of the review pursuant to article 7(5).
46. I further affirm its decision to withhold records 3, 5, 5(a), 6, 9 and 9(a) pursuant to article 9(1)(b) of the AIE Regulations.
47. I have found the Council’s reliance on article 9(1)(b) was not justified in respect of Record 6(a). Accordingly, I annul the Council’s decision in respect of record 6a and direct release of this record.
Appeal to the High Court
48. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Gemma Farrell
On behalf of the Commissioner for Environmental Information

title: Mr F & Forestry Appeals Committee
text:
Decision
Mr F & Forestry Appeals Committee
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-300057-A0A2V8
Published on 9 June 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether the FAC had taken sufficient steps to identify and locate the relevant environmental information within the scope of the appellant’s request in accordance with article 7(5) of the AIE Regulations.
09 June 2026
Background
1. On 19 June 2025, the appellant requested the following information from the FAC:
“Information which has informed the FAC's consideration that the rules around State Aid and the associated payment of afforestation scheme grants and premiums are outside the remit of the FAC
.
To include any legal advice sought and received.
Please interpret this request broadly.
Please provide a schedule of records with your decision.
Please ensure that all records provided are compatible with Assistive Technology.
Could you please provide an acknowledgement of this request and contact details for the party assigned to deal with it.”
2. On 17 July 2025, the FAC issued its original decision to part grant the request. Following examination of material held by the FAC administration and the FAC committee the below records were considered relevant to the request:
• Agriculture Appeals Act 2001
• the Forestry Appeals Committee Regulations 2020 and the amending legislation. Both of which are available in the public domain on [external-link https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/ | https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/ ]
